We are now placed in this position-we have to distribute $16,000 among creditors to the extent of over $226,000. The proportion is so small that I am going to ask the government to change this last clause of the subsidy so as to begin to pay the labourers who are still in possession of their time checks, the labourers who have not sold their claim on the road, so that we may pay them at least fifty cents on the dollar If not -more. But I wish to go further and ask the government, when they will take up the new claims of the Atlantic and Lake Superior to remember that these trustees, represented by Mr. Joquin Galindey, advanced money to the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway and the guarantee that they have since 1900 been in possession of one hundred miles of railway which they are working for their own advantage and benefit, whereas the men who built the road, the farmers who gave the right of way, the men who supplied the material and the men who boarded the employees remain unpaid; so that if any money leaves the Dominion exchequer for this Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway or the trustees thereof, the government should take upon itself to pay the men who built the line and not pay the trustees who have taken possession of the road, and thus guaranteed their own advances. I believe that I need say no more, except that I wish to thank the right lion, the premier (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the lion. Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) for the great trouble they have gone to in the effort to bring order out of chaos in the affairs of this road. And, before I resume my seat I very humbly request the government, before granting this additional application of the trustees of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway :
1.	That the Department of Railways and Canals ascertain by means of a public circular the amount due on the Baie des Chaleurs and Atlantic and Dake Superior Railway from Meta-pedia to Caplin, for right of way, labour, board, material, damage, &e.
2. These claims are due to poor people, for the most part labourers and farmers who have suffered through the construction of this Baie des Chaleurs Railway to such an extent that it has become a by-word in the railway history of the Dominion. During the last fifteen or sixteen years, the county of Bonaventnre has gone through a crisis probably unparelleled in Canada; and I hope that before any more money leaves the Dominion exchequer for the purposes of this road, the government will see to it that the people who have built this road shall be first paid before any other payments are made by the Crown or by the department.
I assure my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil, Bona venture) that the matter shall have consideration.

speechtext:
I would like to inquire from the Minister of Railways if the new classification of freight 104J
known as the Canadian Freight Classification No. 12, has been authorized, as is customary, by Order in Council ? The same came into affect on May 1st.

I could not answer the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) offhand, I have no recollection of any recent order passing that had reference to any classification of freight. This may possibly have received sanction some months ago, though it only came into effect this month. I will ascertain and let the hon. gentleman know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
To explain, I may say that the last classification was authorized by Order in Council in 1899 ? I hardly expect that the minister would have authorized another classification on the eve of the appointment of a commission. There are some very radical departures in this new classification. I will read the rule, which has never been applied to any other classification :
When articles are shipped under false names, in order to deceive the carrier, or to avoid this classification, agents at destination will collect charges according to proper classification, plus fifty per cent in addition to the rate which would have been charged had the property been correctly described.
There are 3,000 different items in this classification, perhaps more, and there is great confusion and misunderstanding between the shippers and the railway. This rule, if carried out, means that the company's view of the case in all instances must be the correct one, that they must be the judge, jury and court of appeal, and if goods upon which the freight would amount to $100, were not, according to their opinion, in accordance with this classification, one in which the public have nothing to say, if they consider that the goods are not properly described under this classification, which as I say contains 3,000 items, then they have a right to charge $50 extra on freight which would be $100, and to exact that as a fine from the shipper before the goods will be handed over to the consignee at the other end. I just draw the minister's attention to this matter in view of the appointment of a commission. There are other rules, new rules, in the new classification which are just as radical, and although all the merchandise of the country has been shipped under that classification, at this moment I am almost inclined to believe that the same has not been authorized by Order in Council according to law. If it had been authorized by Order in Council, it would be noted on the classification the same as on former classifications, by number 11, which was authorized on December 19, 1899.

I would suggest that the hon. member put his question on the Paper, and I will have the matter looked into. I do not recollect now that any

recent Order in Council has passed on that subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Before the motion is put, I would like to inquire of the government whether it is proposed to submit to the House the terms of the proposed commission to investigate matters concerning the Treadgold concession, and whether any and what precautions are to be taken to preserve the interests of the public by having them safeguarded by counsel. In other words, is it to be a thorough investigation, or is it simply to be a departmental investigation in which the public may possibly have no rights whatever, and in which the facts may not be so thoroughly investigated as might seem to be rendered necessary by newspaper comments and comments elsewhere with regard to these concessions. The Prime Minister is not here, and perhaps my hon. friend may not be able to give an answer to my inquiry at once. In the absence of the right hon. gentleman, I am giving this intimation rather in the shape of a notice of what will probably be demanded at an early day, and at somewhat greater length, in regard to this matter. I would also like to know whether the proposed investigation respecting the Treadgold concession is to be confined to that alone, or is it to deal also with other concessions in the Yukon which have, in that part of the country at least, caused almost as much comment as the Treadgold concession itself. I think it right at the earliest moment to ascertain the intentions of the government. I shall bring the matter again to the attention of the government, and I now intimate that the proposed commission will no doubt be discussed. At the earliest possible moment the intentions of the government with regard thereto will certainly be asked in this House.

In answer to the hon. gentleman I have to say that it is not possible for me to-day to answer in detail his various questions.^ But I may say that the government is now engaged in formulating the instructions that will accompany the commission. The commission will be comprehensive and far reaching in its work. It will apply not only to any existing concessions, but it will deal with the hydraulic, needs of the district in connection with the development of the mines.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to lay the composition of the commission and the instructions to the commission on the Table in order that they may be discussed before finally being sent out; in other words, will the House have any opportunity of discussing the terms of the commission before it is finally signed and sent forward ?

That point has not been discussed, I will make it known to the government. No doubt, as soon as the commission is ready all the terms will be submitted to the House, but whether that will be before or after the adoption of the terms of the commission, I am not able at this moment to say. If the hon. gentleman desires to renew this question on this subject to-morrow, I will perhaps be able to give him an answer. In the meantime I may say that the commission will not only deal with the existing conditions as to the outcome of any grants, but it will endeavour in a comprehensive way to deal with the needs of the country. For that reason one of the commissioners at least will be an expert, competent to deal with the important question to be investigated by the commission.

If I may be pardoned another word to the hon. gentleman, I may say that it would not perhaps be of any use to submit the commission and the instructions to the House after the terms have once been settled and gone forward. It is within the bounds of possibility that some suggestions might be made from this side of the House which would be of use to the government and to the country with regard to the terms of the proposed commission, and it is in that view that I have made the remarks to the hon. gentleman which I did. It seemed to me, speaking of course with every deference, that there might be very good reason, seeing that this matter has been under public discussion, and a subject of considerable comment in the country, why the government should observe the course which has been taken in some eases, and submit to the House the terms of the proposed commission and the instructions to the commission before the commission has been fairly settled and sent forward.
As I have already mentioned to the hon. gentleman, I will make his observations known to the government, and perhaps I may be able to answer him to-morrow.

Harbours and rivers, Quebec-River St. Lawrence ship channel, $515,800.
This vote of $515,800 is to continue the widening and deepening and improvement of the St. Lawrence channel between Montreal and Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: Would the hon. minister give us some more details as to the expenditure of this large sum ?

A large amount of this vote is for the work of dredging. There are seven dredges employed. It is estimated that $340,000 of

this amount will be spent in the working of the dredges, $26,800 for shipyards, supplies, &c. New dredging plant, scows and repairs to dredges, $113,000, surveys, $25,000, and inspection and superintendence, $15,000, making a total of $515,800.
Would the hon. minister be kind enough to tell the committee at what places it is proposed to dredge the river ?

This dredging is all to be done on what is known as the channel between Montreal and Quebec. There are about sixty-five miles out of 100 that will be widened and deepened, the dredges will be set at work at different places, and they will continue the work that has been going on for the past two years.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say that there are 100 miles to be dredged ?
No, I do not say that.
How many miles does the hon. gentleman say ?
About sixty miles.
We cannot hear the hon. gentleman at all.

It is not my fault if the hon. gentlemen do not hear. I am speaking a great deal louder than is necessary. The estimate of the department is that about sixty miles of dredging is to be done on this channel.
I do not think that my hon. friend, if he allows me, is right in saying there are sixty miles to be dredged now.

I did not say that either. I was asked a question as to the amount of dredging that was to be done, and as to what distance of this channel was to be improved. I said that the officers of the department estimated about sixty miles. According to their estimate about half the work is done, or about twenty-eight miles out of the sixty have been completed to a width of 450 feet, and to a depth of thirty feet.
What is the estimated expenditure on the whole work ?
How much has been spent ?

On this channel already there has been spent about $6,000,000. A great deal of that was spent by the Harbour Commissioners, but on this work which is under consideration now and which is to be continued, there has been an expenditure of about $4,000,000.
And when completed, that will give a channel of what depth ?
About thirty feet.
What width would the channel be ?
Four hundred and fifty feet.
Has the minister under consideration the question of continuing this work to Montreal V
No, the chief engineer of the department tells me that the work of the department goes only to Longue Pointe, and that the balance of the work is under the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.
What are the names of the dredges that are employed ?

If my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) will be kind enough to turn to page 152, of the Report of the Minister of Public Works, for the year 1902, he will find the names of the dredges. They are the ' Lady Aberdeen,' the ' Lady Minto,' the ' Laurier,' the * Laval,' the ' Lafontaine,' Dredge No. 8, the * Baldwin,' the ' J. Israel Tarte ' and spoon dredge No. 6. This dredge No. 6, I think, has been abandoned. .
In this vote of $515,000, is there any sum for the construction of dredges, and if so, where will these dredges be built ?
No, there is no sum estimated here for the construction of dredges. There is a sum for the purpose of building some scows and improvements and repairs to dredges.

I received a communication from Sorel the other day concerning the title to the property that the government has at present for its works and docks. I would like to ask the hon. minister from whom the government purchased the site of the Sorel works or docks, and what price was paid for this property ?

It would be very much more convenient if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) would defer his question until we reach the item in connection with the works in Sorel, and which will be probably reached to-day.
The Chairman said it had been passed.

No, he made a mistake. The item stood for the purpose of bringing down some information, and I will be prepared to give the information which the hon. gentleman asks when that item is under consideration.

These docks are not on the same side of the river as the gov-

eminent shipyards. The docks are on the south side of. the river and the shipyards are on the north side. They have no connection whatever.

At what particular places between Montreal and Quebec is this dredging to be done, and what proportion of dredging is to be done in each place ? Will it give us a channel from Montreal to Quebec 450 feet wide and thirty-live feet deep at low water ? Has the large and costly dredge which we purchased two years ago been working satisfactorily ?

The distance requiring deepening and widening was estimated by the engineers to be about sixty miles, and about twenty-eight miles of that is already completed, leaving thirty-two miles still to be done.
Is this sixty miles altogether, or is it at different points ?

It is at different spots. As to the large dredge, the ' J. Israel Tarte,' I am informed that during the latter part of the season this dredge did very excellent work. It was a new piece of mechanism, the first of its kind in this country, and there were some delays.

How many yards of sand, of clay, and of rock have yet to be taken out ? What did this new dredge cost us per yard ? I am anxious to know that because a promise was given last session that this dredge could work at considerably less than one cent a yard.

I do not know what our experience might be next year, but the report of the department last year shows that the cost was two and one-half cents a yard. I am informed by the engineer that there is no more rock dredging to be done.

I may say that the dredge that bears my name cannot work in heavy clay, and especially in rock. Mr. Robinsou invented a rotary cutter which is attached at the end of the pipe and that enables the dredge to work in pretty hard material. The American dredges in the past were supplied with injectors which forced out water to soften the material, but this did not enable them to work, in as hard a material as our dredge does with the rotary cutter. The work of the dredge cannot be judged by our operations last year, but nevertheless I am informed that in the last month in which it worked, October, I think, she dredged the enormous quantity of over COO.000 yards. It is hoped by those who designed the dredge that she will turn out 1,000,000 yards a month. Her working capacity is 2,000 yards an hour and in my presence I saw her do that, but of course there will be accidents and perhaps delays. The Hon. Mr. TARTE.
estimated cost of the dredging by this dredge is half a cent a yard when everything goes right, but even if it should cost one cent a yard it is pretty cheap indeed.

Has the attention of the minister been called to the fact that some of the curves in that channel are too short ? I am informed by an eminent engineer and by some captains who navigated that river that a curve which was sufficient ten years ago is altogether insufficient today, because the vessels now are much longer than they were then. This engineer stated that if the curves were too short they had a tendency to run the vessel aground on the other side, and that the deepening of the channel where the curves were short was rather an impediment, because the increased depth caused a stronger current in the channel and made the navigation more difficult. This gentleman's idea was that if the money was spent in straightening the curves rather than in deepening the channel it would be a more useful expenditure.

There is a good deal in the representations made in regard to these curves and we are trying to improve them. The chief engineer tells me that between Longue Point and VerchSres there were eleven curves at one time, but now they have been reduced to three. That is receiving the attention of the engineers on the work, and the curves are being reduced to a minimum.

I would like to ask the minister whether, when this work is completed, we shall have a perfect channel 450 feet wide from Montreal to Quebec, and also whether or not he has any map showing that portion of the channel upon which the dredging operations are being conducted ? If so, I think it should be laid on the Table of the House while we are discussing this item, so that we may be enabled better to understand what we are really voting this money for.

The result of this work will be to make the channel between Montreal and Quebec 450 feet wide and 30 feet deep. I think there is a plan, which I shall be glad to lay upon the Table, showing in detail where these improvements will be made.

The maps have been changed year by year as the works have been proceeded with, and I believe these maps are available. The House would be under a very wrong impression to suppose that we have been only proceeding with the dredging of the river. Along with the deepening of the channel the work of straightening and cleaning the river has been proceeded with. When we first took up the work there were numerous curves and other difficulties. The part of the work which has

been completed has been' carried out thoroughly and well. In a few months the works between Lake St. Peter and Montreal will be fully completed, and in such a manner that both day navigation and night navigation will be not only possible, but easy in that part of the river.
What arrangements have been made for night navigation?

The Department of Marine and Fisheries has erected, especially during last year, very fine lighthouses along the channel. There is some little work yet to be completed, which, I understand, will be completed within a few weeks, and it will then be easy for the largest steamers to travel night and day between Sorel and Montreal. This part of the work, I suppose, will be pretty far advanced when this season closes, and the balance completed within two years. The 65 miles of dredging that was to be done three or four years ago will be thoroughly completed to a depth of 30 feet and a width of at least 450 feet, in the straight parts, and more in the curves. When we speak of a depth of 30 feet, we of course refer to the depth at the lowest water, which is only for about two months of the year. During the other months there is plenty of water, and the largest boats can navigate the river without any trouble. When the Department of Marine and Fisheries complete their part of the work, the channel between Montreal and Quebec will then be one of the safest channels in the world ; I say that without hesitation.
What about the accident to the ' Carrigan Head ' ?

That vessel was grounded between two buoys, simply because one of the buoys was not located. At this time of the year, as my hon. friend from Gaspe knows, there is plenty of water in the channel of the St. Lawrence. The draught of the vessel was 26 feet ; but even if it had been 30 feet, there was plenty of water. The inquiry showed that the grounding of the boat was an accident.

I think we should have a map showing where this work is going to be done this year. The hon. minister has admitted the usefulness of that, and I for my part do not like to vote such a large sum of money without seeing exactly what it is proposed to do this year and where. This work is a splendid one, and one in which we are very much interested, and I think we ought to be informed how far it is expected to go towards the completion of these 32 miles this year. The dredge which bears the name of the ex-Minister of Public Works, I understand, dredged 600,000 yards in one month last year ; and we are told there are six other dredges at work.
They cannot all do as much.

They cannot all do as much, but they can do something. We ought to advance very materially towards the completion of these works during the present season. Under the circumstances, I would like to know where the work is to be done this year. No man would think of spending so large an amount of money as this without having that information.

I think my hon. friend is perfectly correct, and he has indicated what information he would like. We all hope this work will go on. How much will be done will depend largely, as the hon. member for St. Mary's says, on the working condition of each dredge. If the dredge turns out as we expected, with the improvement and changes made during the winter, there will be a wonderful difference in the amount of work done in the coming season. It is estimated that with this dredge and the others, there will be at least eight or nine miles dredged during the season, perhaps more.

That will only be a quarter of the work.
The MINISTER OF rUBLIC WORKS. It will be over a third of the work because it is the heaviest portion.
How many hundred yards must be excavated in order to finish these thirty-two miles ?
We have not estimated the number of yards.
An estimate should be made every week in the department. What sort of an engineering department is that which does not make a weekly estimate ?
Lgst year or the year before an approximate estimate was given.

The approximate estimate of the number of yards to be removed is something like 32,000,000. If my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) will look up page 152 of the report of the Public Works Department, he will find the information which he inquires.
In this half million dollars are the wages of the shops of Sorel included ?
Yes.
What was the expenditure of the shops there last year ? It seems to me that it alone ran up to $175,000. What is the estimated expenditure tills year in the shops as against $175,000 last year ?
Just about the same for labour and material.
How much would it cost to fit up the ' J. Israel Tarte ' dredge ?
The total cost of the dredge is $300,000.
What does that include ?
Everything.
What amount did the furnishings cost V I find there some pretty large items, for instance, one leather box lounge, $85.

There were some $30,000 spent during the past season, which of course, will not be given in detail in the Auditor General's Report, until next year, but that was altogether for improvements and changes in machinery.
Is not the cost nearer $400,000 than $300,000 ?
The figures given me by the officers of my department are $307,000, including the improvements done during the past season.

That dredge was built by the Poison Iron Works and the plan prepared by Mr. Robinson. It was found that some pieces of machinery were a little off. Any one who has had experience in new machinery knows that there are always breakages incident to any new work. The piping had been located in a wrong way. It was beneath the deck where the engineers could not reach it easily and it had to be changed. Before I left office I made a thorough investigation in company of Mr. Robinson and we found that some changes had to be made. Those changes have cost some money, but we have now a dredge which will give a good account of itself.
How many miles does the hon. minister expect to dredge of Lake St. Peter this year ?
About seven miles.

I thought so. The estimate given us a minute ago, I knew, applied to the ' Tarte ' dredge, and the oflier dredges should dredge as much as the 'Tarte' dredge should do in Lake St. Peter. I should expect that this year about fourteen or fifteen miles would be dredged. There remains about thirty miles of dredging in round figures, a little less, but let us say about thirty miles. So, if the dredge 'Tarte' carries out the expectations we have formed of her and does between seven and eight miles and the others do as much, there will remain only fifteen to eighteen miles to do another year. The fleet of dredges is now completed. These are all new dredges. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has at his disposal a very fine fleet of dredges, tugs, stone lifters, &c., and his Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
department is in a position to carry out work with a great deal of delight, if I may use that expression. But let me add immediately that a good deal depends upon the crew. The officers of the department will tell my hon. friend that we had a good deal of trouble in keeping all the officers at their posts at times. The dredge ' Tarte ' especially has to be manned with a great deal of care-it is a very complicated piece of machinery, very complicated indeed, and requires all the officers on board all the time, otherwise there will be accidents and the work will not be carried out as the department has a right to expect it to be car-7'ipd out. I hope my hon. friend will take advantage of the first holiday we give him 1o make a personal inspection of that dredge and of all the dredges. He will find that if he goes himself-if he will allow me to suggest It-his presence will give encouragement to the men, and his supervision will add to the quantity of the work, I am sure.

I think the hon. gentleman will have to take me along with him if he wishes me to understand the work. The reference be has given me does not exactly answer my questions-in fact does not answer them at all. Where are our dredges to be placed ? I see that the dredge ' Laur-ier ' last year excavated over 400,000 yards, while the dredge ' Tarte '-probably because it got to work very late-only excavated 93,000 cubic yards.	.
In what month ? That is the work of her first month.

I know the dredge is capable of doing a great deal more than that. But I do not find in the document which the hon. gentleman has referred me the information I wanted. I wished to find the capacity of each dredge by the year or by the month, the cost of operation of each dredge, the place where each dredge is to be located and the portions of dredging that will be completed this year. The minister a moment ago mentioned seven or eight miles, while the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says that we shall have accomplished fifteen miles. So, we seem to be a little in the dark.

My hon. friend will see that I can hardly give him in detail the cost for next year. But the reference I have given him shows the cost per cubic yard for each dredge last year, and it is fair to assume that it will be the same with all the dredges, except the ' ,T. Israel Tarte,' next year. As I explained. if the improvements made during the winter turn out all that we hope, the ' ,T. Israel Tarte ' will do as good work as she did the last month of last year, in fact we hope for a great deal more work and at a lower rate.
How many days did the ' J. Israel Tarte ' work last year ?

Altogether one hundred and twenty-seven days. The ex-Miuister of Public Works probably explained, that as might be expected, when the dredge was first set to work there was a good deal of delay and loss of time. Though the first month's work was estimated to cost something like 8 cents a yard, the last month's work cost only 14 cents per yard.
As to this expenditure for workmen, as I understand the hon. minister, it will cost $175,000 to pay the wages of the men employed in this shipyard at Sorel.
That is for men and material, if I am not mistaken.
It would seem to have run to $175,000 last year for wages alone.

The officers of the department advise me differently. The amount given by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) includes wages and material. They seem to keep the books so as to show both items under one head. I am not able to separate the payments for wages.

I have the document under my hand. If the hon. minister will turn to the Auditor General's Report, page V-35, and continuing to page V-46, he will find the total charges there of $175,000 for last year, and, glancing over it page by page, it seems quite clear that every dollar of that is referable to wages alone.
Hon. air. TARTE. As I have taken a deep interest in the shipyard at Sorel, I may be allowed to say, for the information of the House, that a good deal of the wages are paid for repairs. In a large fleet of dredges, tugs, scows, &c., such ns that which the department has at its disposal, there are always breakages calling for repairs. A good many of the dredges are working in hard material. Heavy pressure is brought on the machinery and there are breakages every day. To carry on the necessary repairs, the department must always keep in hand a pretty large supply of parts and materials. So, there were also new scows and boats and other equipment of all kinds to be built. In point of fact there is a quantity of work that the ordinary layman cannot understand unless he goes to inspect these works. I would be very gTad indeed if members of parliament on both sides of the House, when opportunity offers, would visit these shipyards.
Quite right.

I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) went once, and did not find them in such bad shape that he has much to say about them. These are very interesting shipyards. They are the only shipyards the government
has and perhaps may be a kind of experiment. I would like very much indeed if members of the House, on both sides, when they pass by the thriving town of Sorel, would call and visit the shipyards of the government.
Perhaps the minister would give us an excursion there.

In reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) I would say that if he will read the explanatory foot note, given by the Auditor General as to the wages, he will see that they are taken out of other votes as well as this. For instance the building of the now dredge for the maritime provinces and the new dredge for Ontario come under this heading.
Is a new dredge being built for the maritime provinces ?
Yes.

I would like to ask the minister if there is no special account kept of the repairs on these boats. All I want to know is how we stand. This is a very large amount that we pay out at Sorel. though, of course, these yards are extremely useful. But we would like to know a little about the details. These dredges must have cost a good deal in repairs. What, for instance, is the cost for repairs on these seven dredges which we maintain in the St. Lawrence ? The minister will understand that there is reason for inquiring about that $177,000 for wages. What part of that was chargeable for repairs on these dredges ? Surely there must be a separate account for repairing each dredge. "Again, is not my hon. friend mistaken when he speaks of the construction there of a dredge for the maritime provinces ? I think I have seen a special item in the estimates for a dredge for the maritime provinces.

The wages paid out at Sorel include other items. The chief engineer Informs me, that under the system of bookkeeping at Sorel they could give detailed information with regard to the amount spent on each dredge. I will be pleased to have a copy made of the accounts, showing the amount of repairs put on each dredge. But I wished to explain to my hon. friend that the amount of wages paid out there is not altogether in connection with this vote, but on other works as well.

It means that $175,000 is to be expended by the department next year at Sorel. That is evident from the discussion in reference to repairs to be effected on barges, tugs and other craft owned by the department. I would like to call the attention of the minister to this, that it means the employment of about 250 men every day in the year at $2 per day,

making repairs on boats. It means tliat out of this vote of $500,000 there will be at least $175,000 spent in wages for repairs. I turn to the account of the material supplied last year, commencing on page V-23 of the Auditor General's Report, and ending on page V-12, where it would appear that about $425,000 was spent for materials. Assuming the new dredge, the ' Tarte,' cost $300,000, that leaves about $125,000 for sundry material. May I ask the minister how much it is estimated will be spent the coming year for material or work to be done at the shops ?
The hon. gentleman is altogether mistaken as to the amount spent at Sorel. The ' J. Israel Tarte' was not built at Sorel.

The expenditure is $425,000, and in that is included an expenditure for the ' Tarte.' So deducting $300,000, which in round figures was the amount, spent on the ' Tarte,' that would leave a balance of $125,000 spent at Sorel.
As I was saying, the ' ,T. Israel Tarte ' was not built at Sorel, and the expenditure of $300,000 was not made at Sorel.

Referring to the Auditor General's Report, he will find that the total expenditure on material was $425,000, and in that is included $300,000 for the ' Tarte.' Then the balance of $125,000 must have been in respect to other material that was used at Sorel.
There was a great deal more than that. They are building a dredge there costing nearly double as much as the 'Tarte.'
That was not last year.

Yes, and the material purchased for that dredge alone must have cost a great deal more than that. I was trying to explain that this $175,000 in wages is not for repairs alone at Sorel. It is for building, wages paid out in connection with these different boats, on barges, scows and tugs that are being built, and are charged to the different votes. If the hon. gentleman will look more closely into the Auditor General's Report he will see them shown in detail.
Where are they being built, if not at Sorel ?
The ' ,T. Israel Tarte.' was built at Toronto.

That was the subject of a contract. Now, starting at page V-23 and continuing on you find an expenditure amounting to $425,000. Included in that are a lot of large expenditures in respect of this dredge, the 'Tarte.' I notice one of $137,000 and1 another of $45,000, and others Mr. BENNETT.
amounting in the aggregate to $300,000. If you deduct that $300,000 from the $425,000, it seems plain that there were $125,000 spent for material which was used at Sorel and probably in connection with these different dredges that were on the work, tugs, &c. Would the minister say how much money will be required out of this grant of $515,000, for material to be used by these workmen, whether on repairs or on new work at Sorel this year ?

That expenditure was in connection with the repairs on these dredges that are on this channel work, in construction of the large dredge for the maritime provinces, of the dredge for the province of Ontario, and for scows and tugs in connection with the work. As I have said, I would be pleased to have a statement made from the books in Sorel showing in detail how much was spent on repairs of each dredge.

I may be permitted to explain what expenditures are taken from that sum under discussion now, $550,000. First, the department has to pay for the working of all the dredges that are in commission on the St. Lawrence. This is a special item for the River St. Lawrence ship channel, we have seven dredges. We have ten or twelve dredges, perhaps more than that. We have the hydrographic survey, which I do not think will be transferred to the Department of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But last year the survey of that work was taken from this item. Now there is inspection work, all these working expenses have to be taken out of this item. Then there are repairs, building new scows and boats and all the implements that are necessary for dredging operations.

Can the hon. gentleman say about what that amounts to ?
Hon. Ml-. TARTE. I cannot say this year. But my hon. friend perhaps will be in a position to tell us how much he expects each dredge will spend this year. Last year one of the dredges was not supplied with electric light. These dredges are working night and day. The department has to pay double crews and it costs a large amount of money. There is a pretty large amount of money spent in repairs and there is a very large amount spent at Sorel, because there are other works which are not carried on under this item. For iustance, there is the large dredge for the maritime provinces which is being built there, and which has nothing to do with the St. Lawrence ship channel. In other words, to pay wages, to pay for the maintenance of the stone lifters, the inspection boats, and the hydrographic survey it costs a pretty large amount of money. This work will be completed within the year as it is very far advanced. The hydrographic survey costs about $20,000 or $25,000 a year. That item covers the ground I have just described.

Then, it would seem clear, that, if last year it cost $125,000 for supplies aud $175,000 for these works at Sorel making a total of $300,000, there is left out of this vote $215,000 to be spent on dredging. After that money is spent amongst the different dredges for wages and the keep of the men, you get your return for the work done in dredging, so that, of the total vote of $500,000 for the St. Lawrence ship channel over $300,000 is for work at Sorel and supplies furnished for the boats.

Out of that amount pretty large sums of money have also been taken to equip the shipyards and to complete buildings. In the shipyards there are always new implements required as any one who is familiar with mills and machinery knows. Out of that amount all these things have had to be bought in the past and I suppose this year the hon. Minister of Fublic Works will be also obliged to buy new implements. There is always something required in connection with a big work of that kind.
We hope that the dredge ' J. Israel Tarte ' will work satisfactorily as the result of the changes and if so we expect to reverse the figures and that at least $350,000 will be spent on dredging.

I do not understand what the hon. gentleman means, because the improvements will not give any more capacity to the dredge. There are only some piping and wheels to be changed. That will not add to the capacity of the dredge at all. If the hon. minister will give some attention to the subject he will find that the changes have nothing to do with the question. If the dredge ' Tarte ' does a million yards a month it will be so much the better, but the wages of the crew are the same whether the dredge does a large amount of work or does a less amount of work. The wages were the same last year. Unfortunately some of the machinery broke down, but the wages had always to be paid, so that it does not affect the expenditure at all. The expenditure will be the same whether the dredge works well or not, but what the hon. minister means, I suppose is, that if the dredge answers our expectations a much larger amount of work will be done, and the dredging will cost less, but the expenditure will be the same.

I made both statements and I think I am strictly correct. If the dredge works satisfactorily we will accomplish a great deal more work. If the dredge works five or six months instead of 100 days it will cost more money, as the ' Tarte ' consumes forty tons ot coal per day, but we will get more work.

Here is an item that I would like a little explanation on :
A. W. Robinson, consulting engineer, four days time at Ottawa, consultation, $40 per day	$160 00
Journey to maritime provinces, to examine conditions under which proposed dredging will be done, and report on same, four days at $40 ; fare
$40.50 ; sundry outlay, $25.25	 225 75
One day at Sorel on shipyard improvements, $40; expenses, $4, April 2, 1900.	44 00
One day's time at Sorel, consultation.. 40 00
It seems to me that this is a very large amount to pay-$40 per day-for a consulting engineer. Perhaps the hou. minister can give us some explanation of that.
The only explanation I can give is that the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) saw fit to engage a gentleman of talent and experience and probably bad to pay him for his services.
Is he in the employ of the department all the time or is he specially employed ?
No, he has been the consulting engineer to the department.
Who is he ?
Sir. Robinson.
What are his qualifications ?
He is from Montreal.

Last year of the $500,000 voted something like one-half of it was to be expended an this way : To build a tug, $25,000; two large dump scows, $26,000; completion of one scow, $4,000; construction of one flat scow with boiler. $7,000; construction of one saw-mill, $15,000; construction of equipment of marine railway, workshops and shipyard, $20,000 ; refitting shipyard, $5,000; rebuilding wharf, $3,000; and unforeseen expenses, $30,000. Take these items from the $500,000 voted last year and you will get what the hou. gentleman would expend iu dredging during the past year. The year previous there were about sixty miles of channel to be dredged and ten miles of that was dredged out of the $500,000 vote of last year. Now, the hon. minister has increased the vote from $500,000 to $515,000. What I want to know is if all the works that the money was voted for last year have been completed. If they are, the hon. gentleman will have a much larger sum this year for the purpose of dredging.

The expectation is that we will be able to spend a very much larger sum on the dredging out of this total estimate-$340,000 or $350,000 we think will be spent. Some of these works the hon. gentleman has mentioned are completed and some are under construction.

I asked the hon. gentleman the names of the dredges. In answer

to another question the hon. gentleman said that dredging cost per yard something like two cents and a fraction. We have a dredge here which does the work at one cent a yard and others which do it at three or four cents a yard. What is the cost per yard of each of the dredges.

That, of course, altogether depends on what kind of material the dredges are working in. Some work costs less than three cents a yard, and in some other cases it would run nearly up to seven cents a yard. In the case of this dredge the first month the average cost was as high as eight cents a yard and the last month she worked it was a little less than one and one-half cents a yard, giving an average cost of two and one-quarter cents.
In spite of the fact that the dredge ' J. Israel Tarte ' was new and did not work all the time, what amount of dredging did she do last year ?
One million nine hundred and sixty-one thousand two hundred and fifty yards.
So that the House may understand the great improvement that this dredge is, would the minister say what amount was done by all the other dredges ?

The other dredges altogether turned out a little over 2,500,000 yards. If the dredge ' Tarte ' is in good working order this season it ought to handle as much material as the other six, or about 2,500,000 yards.

Of course, this does not prove that the other dredges are not good; they are simply of a different pattern. The ' Tarte ' is a suction dredge destined to work in sand or in light clay while the other dredges are elevator dredges with buckets, and are intended for heavier dredging. I have seen one of the other dredges working for hours and hours at a piece of rock which afterwards we had to remove with a stone lifter. These other elevator dredges are fine dredges indeed; they are about the best of the kind on the continent of America, but their capacity cannot be estimated by the capacity of the ' Tarte,' which is a different kind of dredge altogether. The dredge which we are building for the maritime provinces will be both a suction dredge and an elevator dredge combined.
To get any fair idea of the capacity of the different dredges we would have to know what amount of work each one would do working in the same kind of material.
That is so.
The average capacity of these dredges is between 5,000 and 0,000 yards a day, or about 8.000 yards night and day.
What is the cost of one thousand yards of dredging done by the government dredges as compared with the cost of one thousand yards done by the contract dredges ?
It would be about two-thirds less by the government dredges.
Do I understand that the construction of dredges is practically done now ?
No.
What dredges are not completed ?
We are building a large dredge for the maritime provinces. Are you referring to the dredges that are working on this channel ?
Yes.
They are all completed.
Is it expected that this dredging will remain with the Department of Public Works ?
Yes.

When these items were being discussed before, we heard a great deal about the division of the departments; are ail the dredges on the St. Lawrence to continue under the management of the Department of Public Works ?
Yes.
What dredges, if any, have been taken out of the Department of Public Works ?
None that I know of.
I did not catch the number of cubic yards which the hon. gentleman said would have to be dredged.
I am afraid I cannot give the hon. gentleman a complete estimate.
I understood there was a statement last year that 24,000,000 cubic yards would be taken out of the whole channel.
The chief engineer estimates that in Lake St. Peter alone 10,000,000 yards will be removed.

We have contradictory statements as to that. Last year we were told that the quantity was 90,000,000 yards, and we were also told that the total was 24,000,000 yards. If the hon. gentleman looks up ' Hansard,' he will see these contradictory statements.

I think it must be some mistake. The information I gave the committee is from the chief engineer of the department. I asked him to give me an approximate estimate of the quantity, and he said it would he something like 22,000,000 yards.

As it is contemplated in the coming year to spend $125,000 for material and $175,000 for labour at Sorel, does the minister think it good policy to expend so large an amount of money without calling for tenders for the work to be done ? I assume that during the coming year some scows and probably some tugs will be built there. Is that in contemplation ?

Yes, it is in contemplation to build one spare dump scow of 200 yards capacity ; reconstruction of the upper part of the ' Laval ' ; additional accommodation on the ' Laurier ' for the night crew, at a cost of $2,000; a winch scow, with boiler and winch ; a flat scow, with derrick ; changing the buckets on the ' Aberdeen ' and the ' Minto,' to make them suitable for working in hard material ; a new coal barge, at an estimated cost of $15,000 ; and completion of tug No. 9.

Surely the amount of work which the minister has outlined is not going to keep 250 men employed every day in the year at Sorel-for that is what it amounts to-at an average of $2 a day, though many of them are not paid that much. I think it would be in the interest of the country to call for tenders for the construction of that new coal barge.
The $175,000 is not paid out of this vote, though a portion of it may be. There have been at least 400 men working at Sorel in the past, if there is not that number there now.

I have searched the Auditor General's Report, and I can only find one expenditure respecting the employment of men at Sorel, and it totals up to $175,000. Where is the rest of the expenditure, if it is not all included in that ?

I have explained that that was not paid out of this vote. For instance, there was a special vote for building a dredge for the maritime provinces, and there are other special votes. So that if the hon. gentleman would deduct the amounts of these special votes from the amount paid in wages, the balance would be something less than $100,000.
Would my hon. friend allow me to make the matter clear, if I can ? Would my hon. friend tell ns how much he expects to have to pay for the crews of his dredges on the St. Lawrence ?
I may say that the $340,000 which I referred to includes the pay of the crews and the cost of the coal. I have not the amounts separated.
How much does my hon. friend expect to pay in wages at Sorel out of this item ?
Out of this vote, $125,000 is expected to be paid in material and wages, and the accounts are not kept in such a way that I can give the amount for each. Perhaps it will be about one half.
The material, I understand, is for the building of a scow and a coal barge ? Is that all the department intends to build this year ?
Yes.
Does my hon. friend intend to build that barge in steel or in wood ?
In wood.
What kind of wood, may I ask ?
I understand that it is British Columbia fir.

According to the Auditor General's Report there were $175,000 spent, not for material, but for wages to workmen who were employed in the shops at Sorel. If the report of the Auditor General is wrong, we will have to amend it. The hon. minister says that in the coming season he does not expect that $175,000 will be spent in Sorel for wages, but that $125,000 will cover all the money expended there, including materials for work to be done in that place. We will have to wait until next year and see if he is effecting a saving between $175,000 for labour alone and $125,000 for labour and material.

My hon. friend is quite mistaken, I was explaining what amount would be spent out of this vote at Sorel, but there are four or five hundred merf working there on other work not provided for in this vote, and their wages will be paid out of these other votes. The Auditor General however, has made out the account in such a way as to make it clear that it all comes out of this vote, which causes the misunderstanding.
Then it is expected that there'will be $125,000 spent in wages at Sorel in the coming year.
That is right. It is estimated that the total amount paid for wages will be about the same as last year.

Does the hou. gentleman consider it good policy to build by

day labour and purchase the material, I presume, without tender, for a barge worth $15,000 ?
I think that we have to utilize these shops for repairs and for the building of these scows and tugs, it is good policy to have that work done by day labour at Sorel.
Has the bon. minister any returns showing the work turned out during the past year and expected to be turned out during the coming year.

I have just read that. I have read four or five times over a list of the scows, &c., intended to be built at Sorel and estimated to cost $113,000. There is a large dredge for the maritime provinces which will cost $150,000.
Is the half a million dollar dredge being built by day labour ?
Yes. Then of course there are in addition the general repairs of the whole fleet of barges, scows and tugs.

Here we have the other departments calling for tenders where much smaller expenditure is involved. Hake the Postmaster General's Department, tenders are called for carrying the mail bags a distance of ten miles, involving an expenditure of some $60 per year, yet in the case of an expenditure of $150,000 for a dredge, no tenders are called for and the work is done by day labour by a horde of officials, numbering some 400, paid top wages and hired on political grounds, and the material bought, I presume, without tenders. Are tenders called for to supply the material required for this new dreuge ?
Yes, I understand that tenders were asked for.
Did the lowest tenderer get the contract ?
The chief engineer informs me that it was awarded to the lowest tenderer.
When was that tender awarded ?
I do not say that there was a tender for the dredge, I understood the question to be whether tenders were called for to supply the material.
I understood the hon. gentlemtan to say that this is a dredge which was to cost $500,000. Last year it was estimated to cost only $300,000. What is the cause of the difference ?
The estimated cost, if I remember rightly was $520,000, and I gave the details.

When the department was under my direction, the work was started in Sorel, and I believe that the pltins have been since changed. I believe that this is right. I believe that it is a dredge which is more complicated than any we have yet built, and I think that the first estimate of Mr. Robinson was not so high.
The first estimate by my hon. friend was some $300,000.
What was the cause of the difference ?

1 do not know that there are any particular changes, but the estimate given by my hon. friend must have been too low. There can be no question about the accuracy of the estimate now as so much of the material and mtiehinery have been purchased, and so much work done. I gave the details when the item was under consideration.

The fact is that the cost has gone up from $300,000 to $500,000. The hon. gentleman tells us that a part of the material was bought under contract, after tenders had been asked for. Whether the additional cost was in labour or in material not contracted for, it does not seem clear how the hon. minister can say that there has been no particular change.

There has been no change at all. The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works, as I understand it, says it was a very large work and that the change has been made under his direction on the advice of his engineer.

When I asked Mr. Robinson's advice, he placed an estimate before me, and, if I remember aright that estimate was about $300,000. I concluded to go on with the work. Now, the government has a shipyard at Sorel which cost a pretty large amount of money, so we started building that dredge by day labour, just as a contractor would build it. For, in a matter of this kind, the department is in the position of an ordinary contractor, having its own shipyard. I found that shipyard in existence when I took office, and it had been in existence for years. Such an institution is necessary to the carrying on of the work on the St. Lawrence under the system in use. If the work on the St. Lawrence had, in the beginning, been given out by contract, it would have been a different matter. But when the present government took office, the work of dredging the St. Lawrence was in progress, and the shipyard was in existence. We had only to continue the work then under way. The shipyard was in a very dilapidated condition. The men were working in the rain and snow. I improved the shipyard, thinking it was the best policy, for otherwise we could not carry on there any work of very great magnitude. Moreover, I thought it

good policy for the government to have a shipyard of its own. In the past the government has imported its dredges from Scotland and elsewhere, and I made up my mind that it was better to have Canadian workmen build these dredges here. With the consent and hearty co-operation of my colleagues, I began the erection of these works in Sorel, and also began building dredges and so on. Well, the government, having that shipyard, went on with the work of building this dredge, the estimate placed before me being, as I have said, about $300,000. It is six months since I left office, and I am not responsible for what has been done during that time. I suppose that everything is going on all right but I am not responsible and it is not for me to answer.
I would like the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) to give me one piece of information.
Certainly.
I understand that the estimate was $300,000, and this was submitted to the hon. gentleman by Mr. Robinson and the officers of the department while he was Minister of Public Works ?
I cannot remember the exact figure, but it was in the neighbourhood of $300,000.
Are we to understand that, before leaving office, the hon. gentleman changed the plans of that dredge ?
I did not change the plans of that dredge, but I believe that some changes-some slight changes, not very important-have been made in the plans.
Well, then, if there are no important changes made in the plans, I do not think the explanation satisfactorily accounts for this additional expenditure beyond $300,000.
What does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) wish me to say ? Does he wish me to say that the dredge will not cost $520,000 ?
No, what I want is to have the hon. minister give us an explanation of why there is this difference between $300,000 and $500,000.
The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) no doubt has explained that thoroughly to the satisfaction of my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram).
No.
Whatever the estimate was, I found there had been expended for the expenditure made or arranged to be made up to June 30 next, was $321,000.
How much will be spent up to July 1 next ?
Up to January 1 last there was spent, in round figures, $300,000, and there will be spent up to June 30, $321,955.
Would that include the engine ?
That would include everything.
There were $300,000 spent up to January 1?
Yes, and an estimate in the department that $21,000 more would be spent in the present fiscal year.
Is it possible that there is $200,000 more work on that dredge ? I cannot believe it. There must be some explanation of that.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) must have got the information on the vote for the dredge when it was passed. We spent hours upon it. I have no objection to taking it up again, even in this fashion, out of order as it is, to give information that any hon. gentleman may desire. But I think that no hon. gentleman, even on the other side, would support such an extreme departure from the existing rule as to commence anew the discussion of an item passed some weeks ago after being discussed in such detail. I appeal to my hon. friends that that is beyond the limits of reason and an unjustifiable departure from the rule. The vote asked for $200,000 for the completion of the work. I believe that, perhaps, this dredge cost more than it would have cost if it had been built at a well-equij)ped factory. At the same time, if it turns out as we expect, it will be one of the best dredges in the country, even though, perhaps, it cost a great deal more than the value of it, judged by the cost of a similar work done under contract.
When the hon. minister says that it would have cost less if it had been built in a well-equipped factory, I would ask him if he has visited the ship works at Sorel ?
Yes, I have.

Well, surely the hon. minister will not say that these are not well-equipped shipyards. I have visited nearly all the shipyards on this continent, and I say that the shipyards at Sorel are well equipped. I do not say that they are complete, of course, none are complete.
If my hon. friend will allow me, I would say, that to have this item which has already been discussed

But if the hon. minister will allow me, I cannot permit him to say merely as a matter by the way that I have made a big mistake and that that mis-

take was due to the fact that the shipyard at Sorel was not well equipped. He is wrong on that point.

Perhaps one word, if the hon. gentleman will allow me, will settle the whole matter. He knows that the shipyard is not in a position to make machinery and all that sort of thing in connection with a work like this.
I differ with the hon. minister entirely. The shipyard in Sorel is quite capable of building engines and everything
Boilers ?

Yes, boilers and everything needed in connection with such work. At times, we have not been able to complete certain works, but only because we have had too much to do. But the shipyard is perfectly equipped to carry out any kind of work though we have been compelled to go outside sometimes because of having too much to do. That is the reason why when the ' Tarte ' was built we went outside-though at that time the shipyard was not so well equipped as it is now. We have been equipping it gradually and now it is a very fine shipyard. I do not think the Poison Iron Works are as well equipped-certainly they are not better. And there are hon. gentlemen here who know that those works are a very well-equipped shipyard. I am glad to say that the shipyard in Sorel Is better equipped than that at Collingwood. I have visited them, the shipyard in Sorel is well equipped, and the reason why the work has not been carried out as quickly as it might have been, is not the one that is given now. I do not blame my hon. friend in any way, but it is only fair for me to state that the reason he has assigned is not the proper one.

Am I to understand that, supposing a dredge is to be built at Sorel, for which the hon. gentleman asks $300,000 in his estimates, we are to be told the following year that that dredge is to cost $500,000, and that the money has already been expended on it ? When we ask what that dredge is to cost, I think the officials at Sorel ought to be in a position to tell us as nearly as possible. The difference between $300,000 and $500,000 on the cost of a dredge is altogether too much. I do not thiink the minister has given us a satisfactory answer.

It appears to me now, getting right down to business, that the minister should be in a position to tell us within a radius of $200,000 what the dredge is going to cost. Common sense would tell me that his department should be in a position to give us some kind of a fair estimate, and if he has not any officials capable of deciding a question like that, he ought Hon. Mr. TARTE.
to call in somebody else. I agree with the ex-minister when he places the government in the position of a manufacturer. To a certain extent they can assume that position. But when you come to get into details, there is a very wide departure from the course a manufacturer would adopt in getting his material. It appears to me that any business man, if he wanted a certain amount of material, would ask for tenders, there would be no political'consideration in connection with (it. I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works or any other minister, can they free themselves from all the political influences that surround them ? I do not care what party is in power. The same trouble existed when we were in power, but it is very much worse now, because we can readily understand how hungry the Liberal party was to get a little money when they got into power. All these influences are now at work. Is it possible in human nature that any minister can free himself from the political influences surrounding him ? Can he ask for tenders and get material supplied without any consideration from party friends at all ? Enormous sums have been expended in connection with these works. I don't care for what the money was expended; when I know that every dollar of the public money is honestly expended, I don't care where it is expended. Now we don't want any such erroneous statements made in this House, telling us last session that the dredge was going to cost $300,000 and now telling us it is going to cost $500,000. Why, will any man tell me that any business concern in the Dominion of Canada would be as wide of the mark as $200,000 in the construction of a dredge ? I don't believe it. It appears to me there must be something radically wrong when there is $200,000 of a difference between the supposed cost of the dredge and the actual amount it is going to cost. I do not say that we were always right when we were in power; but is it any justification to say, every time we bring up this question :	Oh, you did it. Why,
Mr. Chairman, I recollect the time when we could hardly go out to get a breath that our friends opposite did not demand that we should do it under contract. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) used to make the House ring with his denunciations, even when ai member of the government went out to breathe, if he didn't do it under contract. Now he and his friends sit complacently and see all these expenditures of money, and not one dollar under contract. They swallow all their professions, and when we make any complaint they reply to us :	Oh, this is great Babylon that we have built, these are growing times. Well, Sir, I am here to tell you that it will be good policy for this government, instead of frittering away the public money, $200,000 here, $60,000 there, and nothing to show for it-for them to reduce

tile debt of this country, the growing debt, they used to talk; so much about when we were in power. There is the Minister of Customs sleeping so complacently. I would give a great deal if I could sleep. It is a sad illustration of how human nature can degenerate. That hon. gentleman used to talk to us so loudly about extravagance that his constituency away up in Brantford could almost hear him when he was denouncing the extravagance of the Tory government. No-w he can sit there complacently.
There was a time to speak then.

Yes, but it is no time to/ speak now. because you are getting the emoulments of office, you are getting $2,000 more than your predecessor, in an office, too, that you said there was no need of. You said the country did not require that office, and you supported by your vote a resolution condemning it. You said that office should not have been created, that there were tco many ministers, and now you sit there-
Chair, chair.

I say the other hon. gentlemen opposite did the same, they supported by their vote a motion declaring the office was unnecessary. And, Mr. Chairman, I want to say to you, perhaps it would not be out of the way, that I can even remember your musical voice-
Order.

I am talking about tlie $200,000.
Mr. DEPUTY # SPEAKER. I hope the hon. gentleman will keep to the subject before the Chair.
I was at the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am in the judgment of the House if I was not trying to speak about that $200,000 that was not expended under contract; and I went back in memory and listened to your musical voice, along with other opponents of- the Conservative government. I was referring also to the Minister of Customs when he used to denounce the old government for extravagance. But now he can sleep, and it is all right. Things have changed, say they, we are getting the emoluments of office, and the other fellows are out of office, and that is all the difference.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

No, Mr. Chairman. 1 think the minister ought to have come down with information. If he had done so he would get his items through quicker. I think he should be able to give us more information with regard to the output. It has been mentioned here this afternoon that the ex-105
penditure at Sorel was something enormous. When we pay out over $177,000 for wages, we want to know what it is for. I am in favour of continuing the establishment at that town, but I think we are entitled to know what we get for the money we spend. The minister should have foreseen that this afternoon we would inquire as to the cost of each one of these dredges, and the maintenance of each one. He has no information upon that point at all. He could have got it by giving half an hour's notice to the employees of his department. We do not know the capacity of these dredges, nor where they are going to be located during the summer. We have no information as to what they are expected to do this summer. If the hon. gentleman had taken the precaution to get us that information he would have saved an hour and a half time on this item. I think, in his department, he could get that information and if he had done so he would not have spent an hour, or an hour and a half, upon this item.

My hon. friend has asked first, the names of the dredges, second as to the capacity of the dredges, and thirdly as to the amount of work that has been done. I have given that information over and over again to the committee to-day.
The hon. minister is mistaken.
I am not mistaken. I have given this information in its various details.
Let me ask the hon. gentleman what is the capacity of the dredge ' Laurier,' and the cost of maintenance. He has not mentioned that this afternoon.

I have answered that question over and over again. Hon. gentlemen talk about getting the vote through. We have discussed for at least an hour and a half an item which has no more to do with this vote than something in connection with the Department of Agriculture or with Japan or any other place, but with the desire to give the fullest information in regard to all these details, I have answered all the questions which hon. gentlemen have asked: yet, we have an hon. gentleman getting up and accusing me of an unwillingness to bring down the information. I would submit to this committee if the discussion which has been in progress for the last hour, or hour and a half, is not completely out of order.
I object to that altogether. The questions that I asked the hon. gentleman were perfectly pertinent to the subject under discussion.

I never said the hon. gentleman's questions were out of order. I said that this dis-

cussion of the expenditure on the dredge ' Fielding,' which comes out of another vote altogether, and not one cent of the expenditure upon which is taken out of the vote now before the committee, is out of order. How can it he in order to discuss'a work for which we are not asking any appropriation ? From my desire to give the fullest possible information in every detail, I did not take the point that the discussion was out of order.

No point of order could be taken. This discussion is quite pertinent. Surely, when we are discussing the maintenance of seven dredges and we And that one dredge which is being built in a shipyard where these dredges are being repaired, and is going to cost $200,000 more than we anticipated it would cost, the hon. gentleman is not going to say that the discussion is out of order.

Surely the hon. gentleman who is a great lawyer would not say, that, while we are considering an appropriation for a certain work because there are other works going on at the shops at Sorel,- he would ask for information in regard to something that has no connection with the vote whatever. It would be just as reasonable to say that if you were taking a vote for building a piece of roadway in Ottawa every other item of expenditure in Ottawa should come up lor discussion. On every item that the hon. gentleman has mentioned I have given the information over and over again. If there is any other information that lie wants I will be only too anxious to bring it down. If the department had been lax in bringing down any information asked for it would only be right that the discussion should be continued, or that the item should be held over until this information had been brought down. But, in this instance all the information has been given.

I must take exception to what the hon. minister says. I have been very moderate in my questions. He has not answered a single one of these questions. He has not told us where these dredges are going to be located during the summer because he does not know.
I do know.
The hon. gentleman has not stated where they are to be located.
I did give that information. I gave the list of the dredges and I laid a plan on the Table that showed where the work was to be done.
I followed the discussion carefully. The hon. gentleman has not given that information nor has he put upon the Table any plan which shows where these dredges would be located during the

summer. When the hon. gentleman says that he has given an answer to all the questions asked, 1 would remind him that I have asked as to the cost of the maintenance of these dredges. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that he has not given that information, nor has he given the capacity of these dredges, nor the results which he expects during the coming season. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that when this discussion began this afternoon he did not know the distance that these dredges were going to excavate during the summer. When the discussion began this afternoon he spoke about a channel sixty-five miles long and finally the hon. gentleman spoke about seven miles of a channel to be excavated during the summer, and which seemed so preposterous that eventually he brought it up to fourteen or fifteen miles. These are details which the hon. gentleman might have known that we would ask for. It might have been expected, in connection with the work of preparing these dredges that the discovery of an extra $200,000 in regard to a dredge to be built in the maritime provinces would give rise to a discussion.
Not under this vote.

It is true that the dredge is not built out of this vote, but there is this reference to dredges and are we going to be to told when we discover that there is an extra of $200,000 for a dredge which was intended to cost $300,000, that because we are discussing the channel of the St. Lawrence we cannot get information as to the cost of that dredge or discuss that point ? It does seem to. put a limitation upon the committee which the rules never intended.

This item was under discussion at a previous sitting of the House and all the information was given in regard to it. That Is one of the reasons why I think I should not be found fault with and lectured. We have spent an hour or two discussing an item which was discussed for two or three hours on a previous occasion. I am in the judgment of the committee as to whether this is not an unjust criticism of me. The hon. gentleman asks for details as to two matters. and although I have given that information over and over again to-day, rather than he should be disappointed or have an excuse for saying that this information has not been brought down in detail, if the hon. gentleman will allow me I will give it again. The first question the hon. gentleman -asked was as to the capacity of the different dredges. The capacity of the dredge ' Laur-ier ' is 1.700 cubic yards. It is almost Impossible to give a proper idea of the capacity of a dredge without stating ihe class of material the dredge is working in. This * is in hard clay.
Is that working nine hours a day or ten hours a day ?
That is twenty hours a day.
The ' Lady Aberdeen ' does 2,000 yards and in ordinary earth 4,000, and the 'Laval ' 400 yards a day.
She has a greater capacity than that.
That is in rocks.
Oh, yes ; but that does not indicate its capacity. She does not work in rocks all the time.
I must give the information in that way. I know it is unreasonable information to ask for, except in a general way.
I asked in a general way, and that is the first answer I got.
Perhaps my hon. friend did not understand me, or he may have been out of the House.

I have been in the House all the afternoon.
The MINISTER OF PUBLli WORKS. As to the point at which these dredges will work, I may say that the * Lady Aberdeen ' will be in Lake St. Peter and the ' Tarte ' will be in Lake St. Peter. Of course, they will have to work over nine or ten miles of ground.
Will the ' Tarte ' start from the point where she left off last year ?
Yes.
And the ' Lady Aberdeen ' will start from the lower part of the lake, going up ?
Yes.
Is it not expected that the Lake St. Peter dredging will be completed this year with these two dredges at work ?
The engineers do not think they will be able to complete that work this season.
How many miles will the ' Lady Aberdeen ' be expected to cover ?
The ' Lady Aberdeen ' is sent there to prepare the work where the ' Tarte ' is located.
Will they both work on the same spot ?

Not at the same time. The engineer tells me that they will put the ' Lady Aberdeen ' 105J
there to make a depth for the ' Tarte ' to work on.
I do not understand that at all. I have been at that place many times, and they did not do that last year.
The engineer informs me that we are doing exactly the same as we have done last year.
Is the crew on board the ' Tarte ' the same as last year ?
So far as I know. I am informed that the crew is practically the same. It has not come under my notice, but the chief engineer informs me that it is practically the same. The officers are the same.
I did not speak of the men ; I was referring to the officers.
The officers are the same.
I hope they will all stand by the dredge and remain on board, and see that the men work all the time. How many dredges are now at work on the ship channel ?
Six. The only dredge not at work now is the ' Tarte.'
Where are the other dredges at work now ?
At Contrecoeur, and Varennes, and Ver-chfires.
Has the coal for the dredges this year been bought ?
No. We advertised for the coal, and the tenders are in now.
I want the minister to point out what the opposition has referred to that is not in keeping with this item.

I am perfectly willing to go on and discuss the item. It will, I think, be admitted that the discussion should be confined to the object for which the money is used, and not one cent of this appropriation will be used in connection with the dredge 'W. S. Fielding.'
As the cost of that work comes out of this item, I would like to inquire further when my hon. friend expects it to be completed ?
The chief engineer informs me that the estimate is that it will be finished this season.

Would my hon. friend oblige me by saying if the projects which were under preparation when I left office for the part of the work that was to be done have been completed since ?

333&
I must ask my hon. friend to allow me an opportunity to look into that, and I will let him know.

We had occasion this afternoon to discuss this item of $340,000, and reference was made to the large amount of wages paid at Sorel, part of which enters into this Item. My hon. friend from Simcoe discussed that also, and the minister informed my hon. friend that there were other very important works proceeding there, amongst others the building of this dredge ' Fielding.' It was then that my hon. friend stated, what was news to many members of this House, that that dredge was to cost over $100,000. That is the way that question came up, so that the remarks made on this side of the House were in order.
