Let me ask my hon. friend, if he does not think me too insistent, to give us the cost of the maintenance of each of these dredges, the three principal items of which would be wages, coal and repairs. This was one of the first questions I asked this afternoon. Let me ask what it cost for the maintenance of the ' Lady Aberdeen.'

In round figures, about $30,000. I must apologize if I gave too much information this afternoon, and brought up this subject ; it was not with a desire to prolong the discussion. I certainly did not hear or notice the question which my hon. friend says he asked, in regard to the cost of maintenance of each dredge.

I claim a little merit, because I asked this question at the very beginning, but did not get any answer. I suppose the $30,000 which the hon. minister has mentioned, includes wages, coal repairs, and everything necessary to keep the dredge going during the season ?
That is what I am informed.

When I left office, the department was discussing the propriety of buying a piece of land adjoining the yards there. I do not know whether my hon. friend's attention has been called to the importance of securing that piece of land.
I think we have bought one piece. I will bring down the information.
The officers will understand me. It is a square piece of land behind one of the yards.
The deputy minister informs me that it is the Beauchemin property.

One more question. I do not ask questions for the purpose of creating embarrassment; but we had a good Hon. Mr. TARTE.
many projects in hand when I left office, and I would like to know what is being1 done in regard to them. The Department of the Interior transferred to the Department of Public Works the point there ; the title was ours when I left office, and we had some intention of building a slip there for the accommodation of dredges that were to be repaired. I do not know whether my hon. friend's attention has been called to that slip.
That matter will receive attention this season.
Will my hon. friend be kind enough to let us have the names of the parties who tendered for the coal for these dredges, or state whether the order was given without any tenders V

Tenders were asked for, and after the tenders are opened and the contract awarded, I will bring them down.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Quebec hai^iour improvements, $100,000.
I am not aware that the item we were on before recess was passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declared the item passed and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) then asked what would be the next item after recess.

I am in the hands of the committee, and if the committee want to debate the item further I shall not raise any further objection, but I was under the impression that the item had passed, which impression is borne out by what Mr. Deputy Speaker^ has just said. If any further information be required, I would have no objection to give it on another item.
Personally I have not the slightest objection to the item being declared passed, but I did not understand that it was passed before recess.
I think that the hon. member for Jacques Oartier should accept the offer I have made and that we should submit to the Chairman's ruling.
Will the hon. gentleman explain the item now submitted ?

This is for additional berth room for deep draught sea going vessels along the river front. Here is the plan, which hon. gentlemen may examine for themselves. Representations were made by the harbour board of Quebec urging the necessity for more berth room, and I asked the engineers of the

[DOT]department to prepare for an extension, as shown on the plan laid on the Table, of 462 feet long and 40 feet wide at the base. I advertised for tenders and several were received, and the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderers, Messrs Dusseault and Lemieux, or LSvis, for $198,700. The contract was awarded to them on the 8th of May.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to suggest that it was at the request of the harbour commissioners that the plans were changed ?
It was on' the representations made by the harbour board that the plan now on the Table was prepared.

This is not an answer, and I must insist on a clear 'answer. The Pl;| ns on which I advertised for public tenders were prepared by the department with the co-operation of the harbour commissioners at Quebec. These gentlemen came to Ottawa with the board of trade and interviewed the right hon. gentleman and myself, and the government decided to go on with the work. Money was asked and voted by the House. During the last session of parliament I laid on the Table of the House the plans on which these tenders were to be asked, and I say again that these pJans, after being prepared by the department were submitted to the harbour board and approved by thefo. So I understand the bon. minister to say that these large plans- for the plans for which I advertised were for much larger works than those now proposed to be carried out-were abandoned at the request of the Quebec harbour board.

What reasons may have influenced them I do not know, blit when I took office the representation made by the harbour board to me was that the plan at present submitted was the one they wished carried out. I am not seeking to avoid the hon. gentleman's question, but simply to say that representations made both in writing and personally by the president, engineers and other representatives of the harbour board were iu favour of these plans. I am not prepared to say whether the harbour board had a meeting or not, and formally decided to ask to have these new plans substituted for the other, but they did ask that this plan be adopted at the present time, and they also made suggestions to me which I will explain when the plans they have suggested and which are a little different from the original plan are discussed.

What surprises me is the statement that the harbour board suggested smaller works, after they had approved of the plans on which tenders were asked. Of course, I have not one word more to say. But I have asked for the correspondence and I do not know whether it has been brought down.
The chief engineer informs me that the correspondence has been brought down.
I understand that the minister is doing this preliminary work, and that later on further provision will be made, if the trade requires it ?
Yes.
Are further works in contemplation in the port of Quebec ?
No, no other representations have been made to me, nor any other plans submitted.
Because, there was some difficulty about that work. Other parties wanted the work to be made elsewhere. But I am fully satisfied with the explanation.
No further representations were made to me. The change in the larger plan as suggested by the harbour board was to extend four or five hundred feet or perhaps further to deep water before turning.
In fact only part of the larger works that would have been carried on are applied for this year ?
That is all.

Is there any request from Quebec looking to the deepening of the harbour ? I understood that the water was not quite deep enough for some of the larger vessels that come into the St. Lawrence ? ' The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. No representations have been made, unless they were made some time ago. Nothing of that kind has been brought to my notice.

I suppose wliat my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr Kemp) refers to is the Louise basin ? It is very difficult to dredge deeper there, because the wharfs are built in such a way that if you dredge deeper they will tumble.
I was told by a gentleman who conies from Quebec Jliat there is a difficulty about docking. That is why I asked the question.
This will give them about forty or fifty feet of water. Outside of the basin I think they have about thirty feet. The matter has not been brought to my attention.
Would the hon. minister kindly tell me how many tenderers there were and from whom, if he has the information at hand 1

I cannot speak with certainty from memory, but I believe there were five or six tenders, including one from M. P. Davis, or Davis Bros., the Connollys, Poupore-almost all * the large contractors who have a plant.
How much additional space would these improvements give ?
Ill round figures, 500 feet. The actual wharf is 460 feet.
That is in one direction. How long is it in the other '!
It is straight out to deep water. It is left so that in the future, if we decide, we can either go further or return as by the plans formerly made.
How many feet of water will be inside the works ?
The figures are given on the plan. It is shallow water.
The dredging will not be carried out now ?
Not at present.
So, there will be only one berth wharf for a large ship ?
So far as I am concerned, the question with the department is whether we should extend this from 400 to 600 feet and then return.
The plans formerly decided on gave a large basin, and three berths. These reduced plans, will be a good improvement, however, though not quite so useful as the others would have been.

I remember seeing last year in ' Le Soleil,' the government organ in Quebec, that very extensive improvements had been formally decided upon in the harbour there, to cost several hundred thousand dollars, that the improvements had been approved of, the plans sanctioned and work to begin immediately. I believe the names of the successful tenderers were mentioned. The recollection I have is that these improvements had been solicited a long time by the people of Quebec, that they were absolutely necessary, and were to cost over a million ultimately. Now am I to understand that the harbour commissioners of Quebec approve of these improvements which have been decided on by the government, and to which reference has been made here tonight, and am I to understand that they have gone back upon their decision and are now satisfied with this vote of $100,000 and these diminished improvements ? Has the minister any authentic declaration to that effect ? And are these the only improvements which this year will be executed in and around the city of Quebec 1

So far as the matter has received the attention of the department, these are the immediate improvements that will be undertaken this season. It is perfectly true that, as the Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
trade of the port increases, these plans will have to be extended, and it is expected that it will cost over a million dollars to complete improvements that will accommodate vessels of deep draught at the port of Quebec. Probably this is the work the papers referred to. After representations had been made to the harbour board, they decided to go on with this part of the work, and to advertise for tenders ; and I have just read the amount of the contract that was entered into.
Did the minister say that these new plans had been formally approved by the harbour commissioners ?

Yes. Further than that, I say that It was on their representations and suggestions that I carried out these plans. After they were prepared in the department they were sent down to the harbour commissioners to examine and to make any further representations which they wished.
Mr, MONK. Had any tenders been accepted for this work ?
Yes, a tender was accepted and the contract let. The contractors are Dusseault & Le-mieux, of L6vis. The contract calls for the completion of the work inside of two years.
What kind of timber is going to be used ?

Spruce, and either elm or oak. I think if we can get good rock elm it is as good as oak. The engineer of the harbour board of Quebec, who has had considerable experience, consulted with my officials in regard to that. The plans have been approved by the chief engineer. The timber used is below water.

Would it not be advisable, in cases such as this, to make sure that the timber contracted for will be the right kind ? If hemlock does as well, would it not be just as well to give a contract for hemlock instead of spruce, inasmuch as hemlock sometimes finds its way into the quantity supplied ?

That matter was under discussion, and the officers of the department did not seem to think that hemlock is equal to hardwood. We are using concrete where it has to support a heavy weight. Hemlock might last under water for ages, but this work has to carry a very heavy weight.

I would urge my hon. friend to use concrete as much as he can. The ordinary life of timber is not overeight or ten years, and I would advise my hon. friend not to be afraid of the additional expense of concrete. I think he has made a mistake in saying t'hat correspondence has been brought down. The Clerk of the House tells me it lias not been brought down. I shall wait for it. I do not object to the item because the correspondence is not brought down.

My hon. friend must have misunderstood the clerk, because the correspondence was prepared, and I ordered it to be sent over.
I will see that a copy is brought down again.
Is the minister putting concrete upon the'piling ?

This is not piling, this is cribwork. The concrete is above low water mark. I am pleased to say that the improved methods of making concrete makes the difference in cost between concrete and timber very little now.
Harbours and rivers, Ontario-Port Arthur, dredging, $50,000.
Would the hon. gentleman explain where he intends doing that dredging at Port Arthur ? Perhaps he has not the plans by him.
I have not the plan. This is in the channel. My hon. friend is no doubt familiar with the locality there.
Yes, I have been there several times.

These are the channels leading to the docks there through which the vesselmen have found so much trouble in getting their boats. This is to continue the dredging that I think was started a few years ago. Many representations have been made but more dredging is required to allow- large boats to get in. The idea is to make this channel twenty-one feet deep.
What channel ?

In view of the great improvement in the trade of Port Arthur and of .the importance which that port will assume in the near future, has the hon. minister given his attention to the possibility of extending the breakwater ? The breakwater is a very short affair, not over half a mile long, and I think it should be extended to make the harbour what the demands there would require it to be.

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) that I had some representations made to me that the breakwater was long enough to protect the present docks. With an extension of the work there I dare say it would be necessary to extend the breakwater.

I would like to know exactly where the hon. minister intends to carry out the dredging. There are tw-o elevators in Port Arthur. There is the Canadian Northern elevator. There is also the King elevator. Dredging has been done at both elevators, but dredging is also required to deepen the channel. I would like to know exactly what the hon. minister intends 'doing. He has a plan prepared, I am sure ?
Yes, but it lias not been customary to lay plans on the Table.
I do not ask the plans lo be brought here.
This is to do dredging from the entrance of the breakwater up to the docks which the hon. gentleman has named, the Canadian Northern dock and King's dock.

My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) has just said .a word about the breakwater. I was there in August last year and I made an examination of the works. That breakwater which cost a large amount of money, will be destroyed if the hon. Minister of Public Works does not repair it now. It is in very bad condition. I would invite his attention to the necessity of repairing it without delay. It. is being destroyed now. It is a work of large importance. It is necessary work, yet, if it is not repaired, it will not be worth anything. I think it will cost quite a large amount of money, but all the same repairs are necessary.

It is just a question whether the breakwater is not too close in towards the docks. At the time it was constructed the vessels that are now plying on the lakes were not built. Vessels of many thousands tons burden enter the harbours of Port Arthur and Fort William. They find that the sea room inside of the breakwater is rather contracted. I am not finding fault but I merely want to give the

lion, minister a suggestion. In case it should be found that the breakwater needs extensive repairing, or in case that a new breakwater would be constructed and extended in a line south-westerly from the present breakwater, it will be well to place it further out and give more sea room inside of the present breakwater there. As the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) suggests, something will require to be done, and at an early date, or the present breakwater will fall to pieces.

I think we all recognize the importance of the great trade that is growing up at that port and which is likely to grow very fast. We hope so at any rate. The improvements to tiie breakwater and the dredging will have to lie continued. This vote in the main estimates is especially for dredging to carry out urgent work, in fact, I have taken the responsibility, in view of the telegrams received and the representations made as to the urgency of this work, of giving instructions that the dredging shall go on as soon as this vote is passed. The further improvements which are required there will be carefully considered in connection with the supplementary estimates for 1003-4. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) refers to the necessity of repairing the breakwater. There is no doubt that is urgent and when the estimates are brought down we will see that the work is undertaken.
The hon. minister is dredging a twenty-one foot channel. Would he be good enough to tell us in what way he is carrying out that work ? Is he carrying out the old arrangement that was made formerly ?
Yes, I am at present just carrying out the arrangement.
Is it with the same company ?
With the Great Lakes Dredging Company.
Is it the same company ?
Yes.
At the same price- fifteen cents a yard?	*
Fifteen cents a yard.
You cannot do better.

I notice that an item of $35,000 was passed last year partly for the extension of the breakwater and partly for dredging. When that item was up for discussion the then lion. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) made the statement that $35,000 would complete the work. Could the hon. Minister of Public Works
say whether that did complete the work, and if this is new dredging that lie proposes to do ?

I would be very muph surprised to see that the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works said that $35,000 would complete the work at Port Arthur. I do not think that he said that. He may have said that it would complete that season's dredging or some special piece of work that he had under consideration at the time.
I do not remember very well what I said last year. Of course, it depends. There is plenty to be done there.
You made liberal promises. .
As usual.
That is right.

I think this country should not hesitate for one minute to equip Port Arthur and Fort William and all the other important ports on the lakes. We have lost a great deal of time. These ports should lie equipped as well ns money can do it, and they should be equipped now and not wait till we are all dead and buried and in heaven.

This is the statement that was made:
We expect to spend $35,000 this year to complete the dredging necessary.
No doubt the hon. ex-Minister of Public. Works referred to the work that was pressing at that time.

Vessels this fall drawing only eight feet of water grounded in Port Arthur and there was considerable trouble as a result. This increases the rates of insurance on these vessels, and I am satisfied that no one would object to every dollar being expended that is absolutely necessary to place this harbour in a proper condition.

It is quite correct that vessels have grounded in this port, because I was at Port Arthur in the latter part of October, and I saw a vessel which had been aground for two or three days. Dredging work is undoubtedly necessary at that place and I entirely agree that such dredging should be done as to make it a safe port to enter. It is increasing in importance in proportion as the grain trade of the Northwest is increasing. That is true of Port Arthur as well as Fort William. I think the money could not be put to better use than to spend it in making Fort William and Port Arthur safe harbours for large boats to enter.
Hon. Mr.' TARTE. When I went to Port Arthur in August. I found that orders had been given for dredging to eighteen feet

deep, aud I immediately instructed tlie officers to dredge to twenty-one feet. Is there only one dredge at work there now ?

There are three dredges at work.
lion. Mr. TARTE. Belonging to tlie same company

No. Two belong to the company and one to Mr. Booth.
ILon. Mr. TARTE. The three are at Port Arthur, and they are at the same price of fifteen cents a yard ?
Yes.
What part of this $35,000 voted last year was expended for dredging, and what part on the breakwater ?
It was all expended for dredging.

The United States government and the various parties interested, have spent millions of dollars in making splendid harbours at'Duluth and West Superior. At a little place called Two Harbours there has been upwards of $2.000,000 spent in giving shipping facilities. Canada has ports at Port Arthur and Fort William undoubtedly far superior to Duluth and West Superior, and I am satisfied that the Canadian government could make no wiser expenditure of a large sum of money than to equip Fort William and Port Arthur with harbours sufficient to meet the great demands that will be undoubtedly made on them in the near future. I believe that the minister could double and quadruple this amount and expend it on these harbours with profit to the whole country.

I cannot agree with the member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) when he says that Port Arthur and Fort William are better natural harbours than Duluth and West Superior. I am informed bv those who know that these two latter harbours are the best on the American continent. I believe that we should not discuss this question here and now, but that we should wait until the transportation commission brings down their report, and one of the most important things this commission will have to cousidet1 will be to provide facilities for the shipping of grain from tlie head of Lake Superior. Sixty-five vessels stayed at Duluth this winter, and they were able to move grain out this spring at the rate of two cents a bushel. I learn from the grain shippers that Port Arthur is very badly equipped ; the breakwater does not go out' far enough, and dredging requires to be done. At Fort William the river is too narrow, and I am told by men who know, that it will require an expenditure of half a million dollars, and not $95,000, to put these harbours in [DOT]anything like as good shape as the harbour
at Dulutli and West Superior. We cannot expect that the minister will provide this large sum in the estimates now.
Why not ?

Because he is not acquainted with all the facts, and because it will be the duty of the transportation commission to inquire from all parties interested as to what are the actual needs at that point. There is no doubt that with the encouragement given to Canadian owners of lake vessels by the removal of the harbour dues and one thing and another, there will be a Canadian fleet put on these lakes able to handle all our grain. If that he so it will be the duty of the government to spend there half a million, or a million if necessary, for widening the Kaministiquia river and the two small rivers that flow into that point, and deepening the harbour at Port Arthur and extending the breakwater. When the question about the transportation commission is brought up, I intend to give the figures of the expenditures for the past twenty years on West Superior and Duluth : these figures having been supplied me by a gentleman who is well acquainted with the subject. I urge on the Minister of Public Works the Importance of doing something to increase the facilities at thpse harbours.
That is what Col. Hughes did and you contradicted him.

I did not use the term 'natural harbour' in connection with Port Arthur and Fort William, nor can the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) use the term ' natural harbour ' in connection [DOT]with Dulutli, because it is a created harbour. Not very many years ago what is now the great harbour of Dulutli was simply a bog and it had to be dredged out. I have not the slightest doubt that my hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) inclines towards favouring the harbour of Dulutli. It is not so many years since the Liberal party in Manitoba endeavoured to tie up this country to a scheme to run a railway to Dulutli, but owing to the policy of the Conservative party that road was diverted to Port Arthur and in consequence Port Arthur is a growing Canadian town and a credit to the Dominion of Canada. T do not know whether my friends from Manitoba of the Liberal cult have gotten over their discomfiture at the success of the scheme which was promoted by the Conservative party of making this an all-Canadian route. When my bon. friend from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was in the government. I was pleased to find him following the policy of the Liberal-Conservative party in developing our Canadian lake ports of Port Arthur and Fort William. I trust that my good friend (Mr. McCreary) will fall in line now. If one-half the money is spent on our own Canadian ports that has been spent on Duluth and West Superior,

we need not fear the rivalry of the American ports.

It ill becomes the member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to accuse me of disloyalty when a moment ago I asked the government to spend half a million dollars and not $95,000. What I pointed out to the House was that unless we .made Port Arthur and Fort William somewhat equal to Duluth and West Superior we might possibly lose the trade that should come through Canadian ports. The estimate quoted to me shortly before I left Winnipeg was that it would take $1,000,000 to put Port Arthur and Fort William in as good shape as Duluth and West Superior. With regard to loyalty, I do not think the hon. gentleman should say anything to me. Had I done what some of his friends did about twenty years ago, I would have stopped in Dakota or Minnesota instead of going on and settling as a pioneer in Manitoba.
Hon.- Mr. TARTE. Let us try not to make party politics of these broad questions, but discuss them from a broad standpoint. Duluth and West Superior are very fine harbours ; they are practically one harbour. Both have cost a very large amount of money. The harbour of Duluth has natural advantages, which have been improved. I think the dredging alone inside of that harbour has cost in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000. There is a splendid brenkwtater to protect the harbour, and there are practically two harbours, an outside one and an inside one. We can make at Fort William and Port Arthur a very fine harbour. Port Arthur is a good harbour, though it has this disadvantage, that it closes about fifteen days earlier than Fort William. There is an island at the right hand of the port on which the ice jams, so that the entrance to Port Arthur is closed practically two weeks earlier in the fall than the entrance to Fort William. The first Improvement that should in my humble opinion be carried on there is the dredging of Mission river, which would give an additional entrance to Fort William, and prevent the ice forming there so early in the fall and ensure it moving out earlier in the spring. This I think would give three weeks more navigation, and it would not cost a large amount of money. After I took a trip up there I instructed Mr. Coste, a very experienced engineer, to have a plan ensemble-a general plan-made of those harbours. I do not know whether that instruction has been carried out ; if not, I think my hon. friend should lose no time in having such a plan prepared. I am sure that the House would be very ready to vote any sum necessary to make of these two harbours a really national harbour. My hon. friend is perfectly right when he says that Duluth offers advantages which these harbours do not offer. Duluth has one of the best elevators in tlie world. We are having a large elevator Capacity built at Port Arthur and Fort Wil-Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
liam by the two railway companies ; but it seems to me that it is the duty of this government and of parliament to help private companies to do what the United States government does, that is, to equip the harbours. That should be done without any delay. If we expect to get the trade to which we are entitled, we must spend the money necessary to achieve that end.
Is the hon. minister able to state the amount spent on Port Arthur harbour since confederation ?
The tol'al expenditure is $550,332.42.

I think the amount is comparatively small when you consider the importance of the harbour. It is the only outlet for the great wheat fields of the west, where the two railways come together, and it should be made as tine a harbour as there is on the lakes. I think the government would be justified in doubling the expenditure on tWat harbour during the next year so long as they used the money wisely. If the government does less than make adequate provision for the shipping there, they will be criticised.
Is there any general plan of the improvements prepared ?

I have several plans and several reports. I said before, and I say again, that this vote is for carrying on urgent work which is under way at the present time. The whole matter is now receiving the attention of the department. I fully recognize its importance, and should be pleased to have the support of both sides of the House in doing what may be necessary under the circumstances. I slitill be pleased to bring down a report on the subject.
Sir. aiONK. Is the minister able to say what further expenditure would be entailed tinder the pr, posed plan for improvement?
The ailNISTER OF PUBLIC WORK*. Discussing in a general way a few days ago of the improvement of the aiission river, which the ex-minister has referred to,
I obtained a rough estinnate that it would cost about $200,000. I do not say that would make the harbour equal to very large ports, on which millions have been spent ; lmt that is my recollection of the discussion we had a few days ago. when some representatives from Port Arthur and Fort William were here.
The Kaministiquia river is wide enough to make one of the finest harbours in the world when the work is completed.

I should think it would be desirable for the government to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) as soon as possible, that is, to have a general plan made of the harbour at Port Arthur and *

the Kaministiquia river. That harbour impresses one with the possibilities of the future. i understood from those who were on the spot that the river alone could be utilized for about twelve miles and that the banks would afford available sites for elevators and docks for the shipping of grain. The river is very peculiar in being more like a natural canal than anything else. It is dee]) and of great width and with firm banks on both sides, capable of affording strong foundations for elevators. There would hardly seem to be *any place which could afford better facilities than that harbour and especially the river I have alluded to. I do not think that this House would begrudge any money for the dredging of the river and harbour in the best passible way. But we should not spend any! money in a fragmentary manner. We should have a general plan of improving the harbour and river after obtaining the best possible advice, and if necessary expert assistance from outside, so that there may be no obstacle to our securing the traffic which is developing so rapidly in the Northwest.

I might point out that in the near future Port Arthur and Port William will be iron ore shipping centres, the same as Duluth and West Superior. I would like to endorse the opinion of my leader and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier in support of some general plan being carried out. In addition the Kaministiquia river has a delta of three mouths which could be utilized very readily iu case of necessity. Then the stream far above this is navigable several miles for vessels drawing fifteen to eighteen feet of water, and with a little dredging the river could be made of great importance. It requires a turning basin.
There is a good turning basin there now.

It is far above that. The Mission river is one of the mouths of the Kaministiquia. Par above that are the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators. and vessels have to back down from the elevators, which is a drawback. I might point out that the old Chicago river was not as large as the MacIntyre and Neebing. The old Chicago creek, which developed the largest inland city on the American continent was not as large as any of the mouths of the Kaministiqnda, Neebing or MacIntyre rivers.

I have heard a suggestion made which might be valuable, and that is for the construction of an iceboat to break up the ice. That would make navigation two or three weeks earlier. The gentleman who made that suggestion told me that in the straits of Makinaw they have boats which break up the ice without trouble.

I have had my attention drawn to the necessity of having an iceboat there, but our first duty would be to improve the harbour. This matter is receiving serious consideration, and I am glad to know that if we can bring down a plan which will meet the approval of the House, the House will not hesitate voting the money.
An ice breaking boat would not conflict with any improvements going on in the harbour.

No doubt, but at the same time it is questionable whether an iceboat would be necessary. There seems to be a great deal of difference of opinion on that point. But the suggestion is worthy of consideration.

If the Mission river is dredged, it will not be necessary to use any iceboats, because the dredging will permit the vessels to avoid the ice which forms on the island and blocks the entrance of Port Arthur.
Yes, that is another phase of the question.
The boats then would simply go by the new channel.

That seemed to be the universal opinion of those to whom I spoke. The Mission river cannot be used for large vessels, and the idea was that if it were deepened so as to admit large boats, that would lengthen the season by two or three weeks.

I have been listening to the remarks regarding the advisability of a large amount being expended on the enlarging and deepening of Port Arthur and Port William, but what guarantee have we that we could thus prevent the diversion of the trade down to Buffalo and other American ports ? Can the hon. minister give ns an idea what quantity of grain goes to American ports and what portion to Canadian ports ? I am afraid that they are expending a large amount of money for the advantage of American ports instead of our own, and neglecting perhaps the channels through Canadian territory, through which grain could be carried to our own seaports.

I do not think that there is any doubt that with proper exertions we will be able to maintain a Canadityi route for the grain from the west. I have not these statistics at hand just now, but I am in sympathy with the view that by means of proper harbour improvements and storage facilities we will be able to return a large portion of the trade for our Canadian routes.

I see that we have spent last year some $20,000 at Port Arthur on the extension of the breakwater and dredges, and some $11,000 were paid the Duluth Dock

and Dredge Company for dredging at the rate of fifteen and a half cents per cubic yard. Was this done by tender or otherwise ?
I doubt whether it was done by tender, as the difficulty is to get dredges. The price paid is the regular price.

Does the hon. minister not think that we are making a great mistake in spending large amounts at Port Arthur and Fort William and neglecting the ports in the east ? We should spend money first in improving channels from the sea to these ports instead of commencing at the back and coming forward, only to find that the channels to the sea are not of a sufficient depth to enable us to send the exports that come from Port Arthur and Fort William out through a Canadian seaport.

The dredging in this case seems to cost fifteen cents per cubic yard. Of course, I know nothing about wliat that cost should be. But it has been represented in the discussion in the committee that in the St. Lawrence the price can be reduced to two cents and even less than that with first-class dredges. If I am right in my understanding of what lias been said on that point, it would seem important, if these operations have to be carried on upon an extensive scale at Port Arthur and Fort William, that the government should take into consideration this very high rate that we are paying and should endeavour to approximate the work as closely as may be to the conditions that prevail in the St. Lawrence.

The engineer of the department informs me that a dredge such as the ' J. Israel Tnrte,' which is a suction dredge, could not handle the material there. The price depends a great deal on the conditions, the class of material and the kind of dredge that is doing the work. I think the rates that we have been paying are lower than those paid on the other side of the line. The dredges are threatening to take contracts from the Americans, where, they say, they receive higher rates. Some material we cannot get removed for less than twenty cents at least. The question of building or buying dredges is well worthy of consideration, and it is a matter to which the department is giving a great deal of attention, making comparisons between the work done by the dredges of*the department and those working under contract.

There are no dredges available on the Canadian side of the lakes. I know them all. They are good dredges, but not modern ; they are spoon dredges. But there is no doubt that, with an elevator dredge, the Kaministiquia and the Mission river and Tort Arthur could be dredged at a rate of two or three cents a yard. In Mr. CLARKE.
former days, there was a government dredge, No. 6 I think it was, which carried on dredging at two cents a yard at Fort William, and I make bold to say that if one of our dredges on the St. Lawrence could be sent up there-of course, it cannot be done-the dredging could be done there for less than two cents a yard. There is no possible doubt about that. I know that the department require spoon dredges to dredge near the wharfs, but the modern elevator dredges can work elsewhere. The department, in my humble opinion, could equip itself with one or two of these spoon dredges also. But in such dredging as that in the Kaministiquia or the Mission river, one elevator dredge could do more work than three or four of these dredges for which we pay fifteen ceuts a yard. That is the whole story in two words. But they are not available, so the minister cannot help himself.
What is the dredging in the Kaministiquia. I understood it was only soft material brought down the river.
There is a good deal of soft stuff in the Kaministiquia, but there is hard material below it. If we had a large suction dredge, I understand it could do the work in the Mission river.
How much would an elevator dredge cost ?
In round figures-$100,000 or $125,000.
It depends on the size.

The trouble is to get dredges. Some of the dredges that were under commission last year at the present rate told us that they could get better rates on the other side of the line, and we are in a position where we must make the best possible bargain. We have arranged at present to continue under the old arrangement

Does not all this prove that what we require is a broad, comprehensive plan and also a modern equipment ? There is only one way to do this thing, and that is to do it. The country will be quite willing to bear the expense. It is far better to have improved dredges and get the work done, than to fritter away the money of the people on a small and imperfect plan. Why should not the government take the responsibility of coming down with a plan for the improvement of these harbours, and, if necessary, provide the government dredges to carry out the work ? The result of this would be that we should actually get harbours improved and the work would be done at the lowest cost.

But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) must not lose sight of the fact that the work on the St. Lawrence
l

ship channel will soon be completed. On a visit I paid to the lakes and harbours last year, I instructed Mr. Coste to prepare a general plan for the improvement of the harbours, and the rivers as well, from a Canadian standpoint. My intention was to come before the House with a report showing what, in my humble opinion and in the opinion of the officers of the department were the most pressing works to be carried out. The completion of the works on the St. Lawrence will set free a powerful fleet of dredges, and these dredges can work on the lakes. So, perhaps, we should not hurry too much in building new dredges. But, for the time being, it seems to me that the thing to be done is to prepare a careful plan not only covering Port Arthur and Fort William, but covering the whole system because it will be of no use if we carry out improvements at the head of the lake only. My hou. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) said that a great deal of our trade is diverted to American ports. The reason is obvioifs-these American ports are splendidly equipped. Duluth, Milwaukee, Chicago, West Superior, Buffalo are all magnificently equipped, while we have on the great lakes not one single harbour which can be called properly equipped. We have only the beginning of an equipment on any harbour on the lakes. We must equip the port of Montreal and all the harbours if we expect trade to be carried through them. It is all very well to say : Let us have improvements in the west; let us have more railways. I altogether share the views of my hon. friend from Lunenburg. Unless we equip our harbours on the lakes, the Canadian trade will not go through Canadian channels. Nobody who knows anything about the carriage of trade can fail to understand that the time will never come when an all-rail route will supersede the waterway. That is out of the question. So I cannot too strongly urge upon the Minister of Public Works to give his personal and immediate attention to the important question of equipping our waterways and our harbours on the lakes and on the St. Lawrence. That is a national question.

When does the Minister of Public Works expect this dredge to be completed ? When the vote was asked for, it was supposed $300,000 would complete this dredge, hut the Minister of Public Works tells us to-day that it is going to cost $500,000, and at the same time he tells us that from the last of December to the 1st of .Tune there has been expended $20,000 on it. At that rate it will take twenty-five years to finish this dredge.
My hon. friend is mistaken. But I would say to him that we have fully discussed this question, and he can look up the report and see what was said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask members of the committee not to diverge from the general question of transportation.
What was the amount paid per cubic yard last year ?
Fifteen and fifteen and a half cents.
At that rate the contractors must have made a fair profit. I suppose it is understood that we are not going to pay any more than fifteen or fifteen and a half cents a yard this year ?
Not if we can make a contract at that price.
I was up the St. Mary's river last year and inquired what was being paid for dredging, and my information was that it cost thirteen cents.
That may be quite correct. A dredge may make more money at thirteen cents in some localities than at forty cents in others.
Who is the engineer on these works, and who are the inspectors ?

Mr. Temple is the engineer. I cannot give the names of the inspectors.
St. Andrews Rapids improvements, Red river,
This is to carry on works under contract at St. Andrews rapids. I find on investigation that the progress is rather slow. On the contract itself something like $28,000 or $30,000 only has been spent.

Has not the life of that contract nearly expired ? Practically the work has not started yet. This is practically all a revote of the item of last year. I hope the minister will tell us what course ho is going to follow to secure the early completion of that work.

The amount of the contract is $169,000. The cost of the land, engineering and that sort of thing, is put down at $47,000. The time for the completion of the contract will expire during this summer. There has probably been good reason for the delay.
What are the reasons ?

Representations were made asking for a change in the contract. I think my hon. friend will remember that the first year there was high water, floods had something to do with the delay. I have been looking over the matter, but have not come to a decision yet to recommend a change in the contract. I think tliev first started work in 1901-2.
What were the changes they asked for ?	,	j

If I remember right, they asked to have concrete work changed to stonework. Representations were made that solid concrete work would not stand so well as stone work in that climate subject to extremes of heat and frost. I have asked for a report from the engineers on this subject.
ITon. .Mr. TARTE. The true reason why that work has not proceeded more rapidly is because the contractor took it at too low a price. I do not know what may have induced him to take that contract at the price lie named. His tender was a regular one, he made a deposit and I signed the contract, He had been a contractor on the Canadian Pacific Railway on a large scale, and he made a deposit in the neighbourhood of $50,000, so I had nothing else to do than to sign the contract. But all the same, the price was too low, and it was not long before lie asked to change the concrete to stone work. When my hon. friend has been Minister of Public ^Vbrks for a longer time, he will find that whenever a contractor takes a contract at too low a price, it will not lie long before he will ask for changes. Tlie Messrs. Kelly, very able contractors, asked for changes. They stated that in their opinion it was better to have stone than concrete. Of course anybody who knows anything about works of that kind is aware that concrete is better than stone in that climate. I declined to make the change. 1 said to Mr. Kelly, 1 will do everything I can to help you out, I will not be unduly hard with you, but I cannot consent to that change. The hon. Minister of Public Works has just said that perhaps the demand for these changes has been a cause of delay, but I gave him a very clear answer, on .the report of the officers of the department, of course, and other engineers with whom I consulted, that the changes could not possible: be made, that I could not take upon myself to recommend to my colleagues that these changes should be made which would have increased the cost by a quarter of a million dollars. I could not possibly have entertained that suggestion for one minute. I said :	If you want to give up your contract, I will ask my colleagues to give you back your deposit, although, in the ordinary course of business, we should confiscate it. That contractor cannot possibly carry out this work without a great loss of money.
Has he done any work ?

lie has done very little work indeed. If parliament will insist upon a contractor losing money it has a right to do so. We have a right to exact from him that he will carry out his contract. We should say to him : You must either carry out your work or give it up. He did not carry out the work and he did not give it up. He waited but I declined to make the changes. I told him that I could not possiblyr recommend these changes. But, Mr. MONK.
if I had a good word to say on behalf of the contractors, I would not hesitate in stating that they Wave very foolishly taken up that contract. Their price is too low by far, it is too low by at least $75,000 and perhaps more. It is a great pity indeed because I suppose these men acted in perfect good faith. These are facts, and if I were allowed, I would recommend these contractors to the mercy of the hon. Minister of Public Works.
Have any' changes been made or allowed ?

No changes have been made by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works or allowed by me. There have been some representations made by the city and by others as to having water power there. In view of the statement made by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works, I have been making some inquiries of the chief engineer, and he says that this contract is very much below his estimate.
Am I mistaken in saying that it is $75,000 below the estimate ?

About $100;000. That is one of the misfortunes in connection with public works of this kind. I do not advocate it, but if you were to give the minister latitude to say that he would not accept the lowest tender you might avoid a great deal of difficulty, because, when you let a contract under these circumstances in the face of the report of the officials of the department that the work cannot be done for the amount stipulated it only leads to difficulty. In view of the suggestion made by the hon. ex-minister I will take the matter up and be prepared to make a report in regard to it and to ascertain if the contractors are able to go on with the work.
These contractors cannot carry out the work for the price. They must have spent $20,000 but they have practically done no work.

If the contractors stand to lose $75,000, I for my part, would be in favour of relieving them. I do not think we should insist upon the carrying out of works where it is clearly evident that the contractors are going to lose such a large amount as that. I do not think we should countenance any' change from the original specifications. Works of this kind are much better done in concrete than stone and one can very easily understand why the contractors are in favour of making the substitution. I am not in favour of that.
I hope the hon. Minister of Public Works will never consent to this change.

I would like to say a few words in reference to this matter. If i hon. gentlemen will look up the first pub-

lislied report of tlie Winnipeg board of trade printed in 1870, they will ascertain from that report that a delegation was sent down to the government in 1870 asking for the improvement of St. Andrew's rapids. That delegation was promised that the work would be commenced within one year and this was about twenty-four years ago. The m'atter was urged upon the department each year until .18S4, when Sir Hector Laugevin visited Winnipeg, and although I am not supposed to be a very strong Conservative, I attended a banquet given to that lion, gentleman in Winnipeg that ySar because we united on both sides of politics to entertain that lion, gentleman in the hope tlAit he would let a contract for this work. Notwithstanding that we gave him one of the best banquets that ever had been given in the city of Winnipeg', that we fed him well, that we dined him and wined him and sent him away rejoicing, not one step was taken in the direction of proceeding with this work. Matters remained in that form until this government came into power and we hoped that this government would do something. I submit that they have done something. They have made a beginning, but they have made little more than a beginning. As the lion. Minister of Public Works has said, the great mistake that was made was in letting this, work by contract at all. I believe this work should have been done by day's labour. It is a work that one man can grasp and he could easily have looked after the whole thing. It is not like a railway which extends several miles away but it is a work that could be kept under the individual supervision of one man. However, a contract was let to the lowest tenderer and it has been pointed out, that the tender was $100,000 below what the work was worth. If it was $100,000 below what the work was worth at that time with the advance in the cost of material and labour which has taken place since, the work is worth $100,000 more now than it was then, and therefore, the tender is $200,000 lower than the work is worth to complete. Unfortunately, while these contractors were most energetic contractors, while they had been contractors in the city of Winnipeg for twenty years and had built the greater portion of the sewer system of that city, they seemed to have hard luck in the year they undertook this work. The first thing they did after getting the contract w*as to build a spur line from the Selkirk branch of the main line down to the works and the water became so high that the track was submerged. For twenty-one years I have been passing up and down that railway and never until that year had I seen the railway line submerged at four different places. Hast year it was almost the same. The work has been hampered in every shape and form. [DOT] They have done about $30,000 worth of work, they have machinery on the ground and 0.000 yards of sand and they will be out about $30,000
or $40,000. The matter is in a very unsatisfactory condition, but there is no use of crying over spilt milk. The best way for the hon. minister to do in my opinion is to try and grapple with the subject. If it is possible to get the contractors to give up the work then I would have them do so. On the first of July the three years term is up, but as the plans were not prepared until the 1st of October, the contractors claim that extra time, as they say they were not able to go on with the work. During the last six months the citizens of Winnipeg have been clamouring for water power. They find that cheaper power will have to be supplied to the city of Winnipeg and they have submitted a basis upon which tenders will be received for the supply of that power. The nearest source of power on the Winnipeg river is about sixty miles from the city, but it is believed that between 3,000 and 5,000 horse power might be developed at these rapids. The municipalities of St. Paul, St. Andrews, Kildonan and St. Clements, believe that if they could get a bridge across the river at some point there it would be greatly to their advantage and they are willing to contribute a share of the cost. The local government would also contribute. As I understand it, all that would be necessary for the municipalities to do would be to build abutments from the end of the dam to the shore on both sides. I am also informed that some of the railways would like to cross the river at about this point, and probably the bridge erected there might be made suitable for vehicular and passenger traffic as well as for steam railways and electric railways. I have been informed by a gentleman recently, that the electric railway company which is running a line to Winnipeg Beach, would be willing to share in the cost of the bridge [DOT] if they were allowed to cross the river at this point. In view of all these facts, I think the minister should ask his engineers to report on what changes would be necessary to carry out the conditions which I have enumerated. I believe that the feeling . of the people of Winnipeg is along this line.
If 3,000 or 4,000 horse power can be developed there it would be a great benefit to the city. I would ask the minister to give this matter serious consideration within the next two or three weeks, and probably when the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) returns, the matter can be discussed at greater length.
Last year my hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) estimated that the contractors would do $250,000 worth of work this year.
I hoped so.

If they have only done $30,000 worth of work in the last three years, their attempt to perform the contract does not amount to very much. Is there any difficulty about dealing with this matter ? Does not this contract con-

tain the usual provision that if the contractors do not make satisfactory progress the work can be taken over by the government. I would be the last one to suggest that any harsh measures should be taken with contractors who made a mistake in the amount of their estimate, but at the same time I do not see any sense in waiting for these gentlemen to find that at ti e end of three years they have< only accomplished $30,000 worth of work* At that rate it would take, I suppose, fifteen years to finish the contract. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) speaks of floods delaying the work, hut I would hardly think that the floods have been so continuous for three years that only $30,000 worth of work could be done. When did the contractors come to the conclusion that this was a losing work and have they made any representations to the department ? I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) when he says that the government should deal with this work efficiently and expeditiously. I do not know whether the scheme which he mentions is a scheme which the government should embark in, but certainly something should be done one way or the other. I agree with those gentlemen who say that the government ought to treat the contractors fairly, and perhaps release them from their contract on equitable terms if they are not in a position to carry it on. I agree also as to the inadvisability of making any such change in material as has been suggested, because there is no information before the House from the minister or from his officers which would justify it. In any event it would involve the necessity of a new contract being let, so that everybody in the Dominion who wished to do so would be at liberty to tender for this work. Perhaps the minister would inform us whether this contract contains the usual clause, and whether the contractors have made any excuse for allowing three years to elapse without doing any more than what may be fairly considered as trifling.

It is only fair to the contractors to say that the contract was entered into in July, 1900, the price being $469,000. If. as the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says, the price was too low, then it must be still lower now considering the increased cost of wages and material in the meantime. The plans were not placed in the hands of the contractors until the fall of 1900, so that they have not been three years at the work.
I admit that; it is three years next October.

Representations were then made asking for a change, but these representations were refused and that caused further delay. It was my intention to ask the chief engineer to go there and make a personal report, but with the various works going on and Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
bis attendance here in parliament, it has been found impossible for him to get away. It is also true that the secretary of the Canadian Pacific Railway has made an official proposition to the department, that if a change could be made in the work they would contribute to the cost. It may be of not only local but national interest that such a change should be made. I think the best thing for me to do is to ask the chief engineer to go there and make a full report on all these matters. We have also received a petition JTom the board of trade or the city council of Winnipeg, I forget which, with regard to the development of water power at these rapids. I do not believe myself, that this would increase the cost, but if it did we would have to consider whether such an income could be derived as would compensate us for that increased cost. At any rate, in view of the representations made to us by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, it would be well worth while to see how much of the cost they would be willing to contribute if the proposed change were made. I understand from the officers of the department that the representations as to changing from concrete to stone were made by a petition from the [DOT] citizens of that district. There is a difference of opinion among the engineers, both of the Public Works Department and the Department of Railways and Canals, in regard to the matter. My own opinion is that good concrete properly put up is under most conditions better than stone; in other cases stone is better. To overcome the effect of great changes of temperature, I think the concrete should be made in blocks so as to allow for contraction and expansion.

I observe that some criticism was offered last year in regard to the quality of the stone. I know nothing about that ; but I think the minister has this matter entirely in his own hands. The contract in question must contain the provision which is in all government contracts, giving the government power to take over the work if it is not proceeded with, in the opinion of the engineer, with sufficient expedition to ensure its completion within the time fixed by the contract. We know that it has not been proceeded with with any such expedition ; it has not been proceeded with at all. except so far as $30,000 may be compared with $469,000. This power which the government has is not, of course, to be exercised harshly or tyrannically ; but it is to be exercised in such a way as to protect the public interest by enabling the work to be done within the time fixed by the contract. The department may take the work out of the hands of the contractors, and if they do, they should deal with th<f contractors fairly under the circumstances.

I may say. in answer to the hon. leader of the opposition, that the
33C1

336Z
reason I did not exercise the right which the government undoubtedly have to take the contract from the Messrs. Kelly Brothers, was that every time we wrote to' them and warned them that they were not carrying out the work, they invariably answered that they would go on with it. They were men of reputation, who had carried out very large works elsewhere, and it was pretty difficult for'the department to say to such men : We have no confidence in you. The last time I told them very firmly that I could not grant the changes which they asked for, and I added that if they would not go on with the work I would cancel the contract immediately. Then Mr. Kelly told me that even if he lost $100,000, he would carry out the work. His words to me were : ' I have never failed to carry out a contract yet, and I will carry out this one.' The hon. minister says that since I left office the department has received an intimation from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that they will contribute towards the work if certain changes are made.
We have a proposition in writing.
I understand that if that proposition is accepted by the government, new tenders will be asked, because it will be a new work.
Certainly.
As to changing from concrete to stone, I do not know whether I correctly understood the hon. minister to say that there was a difference of opinion on the subject in the Department of Public Works.

I said among the engineers. The hon. gentleman must know from his experience that engineers differ- in opinion as between stone and concrete ; but I said that in my own experience good concrete, if properly put in, was better under certain conditions than stone.

I do not think that any engineer will say that stone is better than concrete ; it cannot be maintained. I know the way in which petitions are got up. The truth is, the contractor is in a hole, and if my hon. friend can arrange with him by paying him what he has spent, say $25,000 or $30,000, and ask for new tenders on the new proposition which he has before him, I suppose it would be the best thing that could be done. That work is of great importance. If the department obliges the contractor to go on, it will take him years to do the work, and he will be losing money all the time. Therefore, I think it will be better to arrange witli him. The minister has in the department engineers in whom I have full confidence, and when he has a report signed by his engineers I have no fear.

It seems to me that this item is in a very unsatisfactory position.
hen we approached it this evening, I understood the minister to say that it was intended to go on with this work. But unless we act very harshly with these contractors, we are not going to force them to execute their contract. I think it is evident that we are not going to hold the contractors to the execution of their contract.
I did not say that it was not my intention to make them carry out the contract.

When the item was first broached, the minister said that it was in order to carry out these works, tlAit there was a contract, but that not much progress had been made, because difficulties had arisen. But I do not think there is any doubt that we are not going to force these contractors to carry out the work as undertaken. The remarks of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), have led me to believe, since the government had the proposition of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company before them, and it would be possible to construct these works in such a way as to make them of assistance in developing power for the city of Winnipeg, that it would be desirable to construct them th'at way. For my part, if that were done, and if the arrangement proposed by these parties were put into shape, I would have much more pleasure in supporting this item. We are now voting more or less in the dark, because it is evident that , these men are not going to be held to their contract, unless they -are allowed to substitute inferior material, and the whole affair is in a state of uncertainty.

The hon. gentleman has just stated that he will not allow any change any more than I did. His information is that the contractors are not going on with the work and he will try to arrange with them by paying them just what is due, and then ask for new tenders, owing to the proposition which was submitted to him by the Canadian Pacific Railway.

I had no intention of doing anything else than go on with the contract as it is, but in view of the statements made here and the proposition submitted by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the department, hon. gentlemen will admit that it is quite proper to ask the engineers of the department to make a report.

I would once more suggest that the hon. minister should try to arrange with the contractor as soon as possible so that before the session is over, a vote may be put in the estimates and new tenders asked for, and the work done as soon as possible.

The chief engineer cannot go himself, but



we have gentlemen in the department who might take up all the propositions and make a report in a week or two.. Then I could ask the contractor either to go on with the work or, if any change is proposed, to come to some reasonable arrangement. _
I did not suggest that the contractors should be paid, but that they should be relieved from this prospective loss of a very large amount.
That is what I understood.
Have the contractors themselves made any proposition to be relieved from the performance of their contract without, of course, receiving any additional indemnity ?
We have received no proposition. The last action of the department was notifying them of their delay and urging them to go on with their contract.
If the contractors do licit go on with their contract, as it is, new tenders will be asked 1
Certainly.

We are in the same position to-night as we were in last year when this item was up, and I am afraid that we will be in the same position next year. It looks as if the contractors had never made an honest attempt to complete the work. Why there should be a mistake, I cannot understand, because tenders were called for twice, and when they found they could not do the work, without even making a fair start at it, there must have been something more than a mistake. As regards the changing from concrete to stone, the hon. minister says that petitions came from Winnipeg for that change, but these were based on the fact that there is native stone available, and the petitioners asked the department to decide whether a change could be made without detriment to the work. What the city of Winnipeg wants is not that the specification should be changed, but that the work should be proceeded with. They do not want to injure the contractor, but the work should not be held back when he is altogether in fault.
The only promise I can make is that one I have made. I will take the best talent I have in the department and have a report made before the session closes.

I understand that there is an offer from the Canadian Pacific Railway and the city as well, and I would suggest that this power should not be allowed to fall into the hands of a private individual or even the Canadian Pacific Railway.
The proposition of the Canadian Pacific Railway is not to get the power, but propose that if certain changes are made, they will contribute to the cost.

In answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg, I may say that I never hinted that a mistake was made. I only said'that the Kelly's had tendered too low. They never said that they had made a mistake in their specifications or in any part of their tender.

It appears to me that it would be better to settle with the contractors in default before undertaking the larger scheme. If you send out an engineer and have it understood that you are abandoning the original scheme, then you will find that the government, instead of the contractor, will be in the position of having made default. The contractor will then say :	I have expended $30,000, and I have
a large quantity of plant and material on the ground, and if the government is going to take this matter out of my hands, I will be entitled to compensation. The minister should at once notify these men to proceed with their contract and put them in default before entertaining any of these larger propositions suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk and others. Otherwise they will find that, great as is the difficulty, we| are in at present, still greater difficulties will surround us.

The hon. minister will find when he visits Winnipeg that the question of improving the Red river to overcome the obstruction at St. Andrew's Rapids is a very live question. The object is to allow boats to go up into Lake Winnipeg and the tributaries of the lake and other water courses, and in that way improve transportation and allow supplies to come down at reasonable freight rates.
And fuel.

Yes. The people of Winnipeg feel it is a serious matter that the work has not been gone on with. They have even gone so far as to say that the railways were, to some extent, responsible for the delay in carying out this work. I am not responsible for that statement, but I have heard it made. These contractors, it has been said, will neither give up their contract nor go on with the work. Is not the contract with the government the same as a contract with a private individual or an ordinary corporation ? Surely the government has the means of forcing them to do one thing or the other. It has been said that materials have advanced very much since the contract has been made and the contracts could not be made now at as low a price as at the time the contract was entered into. Have the government agreed to let the contractors off ? I do not see why the government should act as

philanthrophists in dealing with these contractors who are now in default. At any rate, I hope the minister will see that this matter is settled at an early day, and that in some way the works are gone on with. Even if this work is not heard so much of here, the hon. minister will find when he visits Winnipeg that this question is one of the liveliest questions in the west, and the work one of the most important in the country. I hope that next session, whoever has the honour of occupying the position of Minister of Public Works, will be able to tell us that the thing has been cleaned up and that the work is proceeding as fast as possible.
I shall make every effort to gain that end.
This is to complete the work under contract.
When does the hon. minister expect that the contractor will be through his work.
We are taking a vote for the full amount necessary to complete the work. It is expected that the work will be completed before the end of the next fiscal year.
The contractor is a little behind time, of course.
Yes.
The work was to have been completed by July or August, if I remember aright.
According to the contract, it was to be completed on the 25th December last.
And it will not be completed before the beginning of next season ?
That is the opinion of the chief engineer.
Was not some change made in regard to the material to be used ? Was not one kind of wood substituted for another with the consent of the department ?
Yes. The chief engineer tells me that the only change made was that the contractor was allowed to use a certain amount of hemlock instead of spruce in the foundations -under water.

How many thousand feet ?
106J
Between two and three hundred thousand feet. The specifications, as I understand it, call for spruce, and hemlock is allowed to be used.
Was it not more than five hundred thousand feet ?
The chief engineer informs me that it was between two and three hundred thousand feet.
Was there any change in the price ?
The chief engineer and the department did not consider there was any difference in the value.
The question did not come up at all then ?
It was before my time. I take the information given by the chief engineer, who tells me that the report made to the minister was that the price was the same.
Is it true that hemlock was substituted for spruce for all the work under water ?
The chief engineer informs me that it was not.
Is there any report in the department on that point ?
I do not think there is.
Yes, there is.
There is a report ?
The chief engineer informs me that he does not remember any report, but I will make a memorandum of it, and if there are reports, they will be brought down.

I am responsible for the change the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) refers to. The contractor came to the department and stated that it was impossible for him to obtain all the spruce that was necessary to carry on the work. I consulted the resident engineer and he made the report to me that hemlock was just as good as spruce. I consulted the chief engineer and he told me the same thing. I do not remember whether there is a written report from him, but I think there is. If my hon. friend will be good enough to look, he will find that there is one report at least. The change was made only for the interior of the foundation, what I may call the cross section. As hemlock was just as good as spruce and as we were anxious to get the work proceeded with as speedily as possible, I allowed the change. But there is certainly a report.

If the hon. minister will allow us to have the report, I shall be glad.
I understand that in these works there are very heavy blocks of concrete over the hemlock foundation. Is that the case ?
Yes.

I would like to ask the minister, in connection with this item if anything has been decided with regard to the dry dock in the vicinity of where this pier is being built, or is that matter still in the same condition as it was a year or two ago.
No decision has been come to with regard to that matter.
May I ask the minister what is the difference between the price of spruce timber and hemlock ?
I cannot say from my personal knowledge, but I am told that at Montreal there is no difference in price.
I have a subject matter I would like to bring up that is allied to this transportation question; I refer to the improvements in Summerside harbour that were started some three or four years ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid we cannot take up Summerside harbour.
But there is no other item in the estimates on which I could bring it up.
There will be an item, and my hon. friend will have an opportunity of discussing Summerside harbour when I will be in a better position to give him information.
I think it is perfectly in order for my hon. friend to discuss the absence of an item.
I was suggesting that I would be in a much better position to give him information when the supplementaries come down. I know what he refers to, it is one of these unfortunate contracts.

At an earlier period of the session the minister promised to bring down the correspondence in connection with this matter; I do not think it has been tabled yet. I would like to have that correspondence down before the item comes up in the supplementaries.
The correspondence I have promised is being prepared, and will he laid on the Table perhaps to-morrow.

Did I understand the minister to say that there will be an item I Hon. Mr. TARTE.
in the supplementary estimates for Summer-side breakwater ?

That is my intention.
Port Colborne-harbour improvements, $142,000.
This sum is to complete the work under contract at Port Colborne.
When the work is completed what will be its length and width ?
It will be fifty feet wide and 5,700 feet long, including a head block 100 feet by 60 feet.

In the original contract, was the width of the structure to be tweuty: five feet or, fifty feet ? And if there was a change from twenty-five to fifty feet, was that the subject of extras, or was there a new contract for the additional work ?

The original specifications were for a width of twenty-five feet. It was found that the work would he too light, and it was made fifty feet. No new tenders were asked for. The price was arranged with the present contractor.
What was the cost of the additional twenty-five feet in width ?
In round numbers, $100,000.

I understand, then, that when it was decided to widen it to an additional twenty-five feet, no tenders were asked for. Was that work performed by the original contractor, and how and upon what terms was the basis of payment arrived at ?
An agreement was entered into between the department and the original contractors.
Was the additional work crib or pile work ?

It was crib work, simply widened to fifty feet. The chief engineer informs me that it; was the same kind of work, only made double width. The original contract price was $395,000; after the widening was called for the price was $495,000.
Was the original work done for a lump sum, or was it done for so much per yard or so much per foot ?
The tender was for a lump sum.

Upon what basis was the widening part of the work done ? Was it so much per yard or so much per foot ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, am informed that the extra amount of

crib work was to be done pro rata the price of the original work.

It seems to me that was a very unfair computation so far as the interests of the public were concerned. As I understand it, the structure for twenty-five feet width had been completed, and after that work had been performed, the minister, without asking for tenders, gave an additional contract for widening the work twenty-five feet more, and the price for the addition was at the same rate as the original contract. As I understand it, this breakwater was to be 5,000 feet in length, running out into the lake. It must be patent that it would cost the contractor a great deal more to build 5,000 feet with a width of twenty-five feet than it would to build an additional twenty-five feet after the first original part of the work was completed.
