He had all the disadvantages in the first instance of placing his plant iu the lake, of driving his piles and sinking his cribs; and in the second instance, he had every facility afforded by having prepared a dock upon which to work. I think the minister himself must give us a better explanation why no tenders were called for, and why the contractor was allowed to exact tlie same price for the additional twenty-five feet as for the first twenty-five feet.

Let me explain that, my hon. friend the minister is in' no way responsible except as being one of my colleagues then. When I was in France, the first contract was signed. Before I left Canada plans had been prepared for a breakwater fifty feet wide. When I was away the plans were reduced to thirty feet wide. If I remember right, four or five hundred feet of that work was performed. When I came back Mr. Coste, represented to me, and the engineers of the department joined with him, that the work would be carried away like a straw if an additional width was not added. We had to make the work solid with stone and all sorts of material. The contractors were not responsible for the plans. They were carrying out the plans upon which they had been invited to tender, but these plans were not the original plans which I bad sanctioned before I left here. The plans were reduced to a dangerous degree. My hon. friends, when they go there, will only have to look at the works to find that they have been distorted. They were very nearly being carried away. Parliament was not then sitting. It was not possible for us to ask for tenders because we were in expectation of the works being carried away. I immediately made an arrangement with the contractors as they were the only parties that could carry out the work quickly .because they were on the spot with all their plant to do the work that was necessary. Any business man would do what I was
obliged to do. It was a case of necessity as there is no doubt that the works would have been carried away. In point of fact the works as they are now will scarcely be able to resist the pressure of the waves. We have been obliged to pay a little more to the contractors than the price of their first contract, but it was a case of necessity. The trouble is that the plans were reduced with the view of economy when they should not have been reduced.
If I understand the hon. minister correctly a total length of 5,000 feet by a total width of 50 feet is now completed, and if not, will this $142,000 ensure the completion of the work ?
This $142,000 is intended to complete the work.

Has the hon. minister's attention been called to the necessity of having another breakwater on the other side of the canal entrance constructed ? The present breakwater and the works of the Department of Railways and Canals will be of no use-I make that statement here and I know I am right-unless there is another breakwater on the other side. The entrance will not be protected and ships will not be able to find anchor there. In point of fact the works of the Department of Railways and Canals have not been proceeded with because the breakwater was not built and the waves are so strong that the works of the Department of Railways and Canals could not stand the pressure from them. Perhaps, before the session is over, the hon. Minister of Public Works might inquire and he will find that what I say now is perfectly right. We want to equip the entrance of our Canadian system of canals. We have, I suppose, received a pretty good lesson. We are not handling very much freight through our canals and unless Port Colborne is equipped it is no use relying on any exchange of trade there, because boats cannot have shelter unless these breakwater works are built, and that without delay. The present breakwater must be considered only as the beginning of the work that has to be carried out.

May I ask the hon. Minister of Public Works what is the depth of water at this 5,000 feet face of dock, and furthermore if any applications have been made by any parties for any use of the breakwater there, or has any use been made of that part of the work which has been completed up to date ?
It is only intended for a breakwater. I do not know that any application has been made for any use of it.
What is the depth of it ?
From twenty feet down to twelve feet.

When tliis work was first launched a few years ago, Involving, I think, an outlay between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Railways and Canals, of a sum exceeding very considerably $500,000, it was anticipated that as soon as it was completed applications would be made by private parties for permission to erect elevators on this proposed esplanade or breakwater.

That is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Railways and Canals. It does not apply to this work at all. This is purely a breakwater built by the Department of Public Works and the amount spent there already, I think, is more than the amount mentioned by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett). I have not the amount spent by the Department of Railways and Canals, but the grain elevators are proposed to be built on the piers to be constructed by the Department of Railways and Canals.

Are the piers that are being built by the Department of Railways and Canals opposite this or in a line from it in one direction or another ? Unfortunately I have not been at Port Colborne and I am not familiar witli the situation there.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) says that the cost of improving the harbour at Port Colborne, including the work done by the Department of Railways and Canals, would probably exceed $500,000. My recollection is that the statement was made to parliament when these works at Port Colborne were launched was that the cost would be very nearly $2,000,000, and I think before Port Colborne harbour is fully completed, as it must be if the money already expended is to be of any public utility, there will have to be a sum in the neighbourhood of $1,500,000 expended there. The breakwater which is under construction at the present time and which is nearly completed, is a fairly good breakwater. I am not, I may say, absolutely in love with it. There was a mistake made at its inception by starting out to build a breakwater absolutely too narrow to withstand the strain of the waves coming down the whole length of Lake Erie. However, that was remedied by doubling the width. The breakwater now as originally contemplated is nearly completed. As has been said by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) it will not afford the facilities which will be necessary for a complete harbour at Port Colborne until another breakwater is constructed to the east shutting off the waves coming from the eastern part of Lake Erie. The piers which are under construction by the Department of Railways and Canals on which to erect elevators are inside the breakwater, which is already constructed and so far as westerly winds are concerned the present harbour is sheltered and it makes an excellent harbour of refuge from western or south-western storms.

May I ask which direction the breakwater runs in-east and west or north and south ?
Jlr. GERaiAN. The breakwater runs from Sugar Loaf Point out into the lake in a south-easterly direction. The piers which are under construction by the Department of Railways and Canals run directly south, starting from the shore line which is 2,500 or 3,000 feet inside the breakwater. The Canadian Transportation and Storage Company which is asking for incorporation this session, has already applied to the Department of Railways and Canals for the right to construct two elevators each having a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels. The promotors of this company are men of ample means, and they will have at least one elevator constructed at the opening of navigation next spring. The Wolvin Syndicate which is called in Canada the St. Lawrence Terminal Company, has also applied for terminal facilities at Port Colborne. I believe that the expenditure of money at Port Colborne in connection with the completion of our waterways will be a very valuable national expenditure indeed. I think that without a doubt, you w'ill see from 30,000,000 to 40,000.000 bushels of the wheat of the west carried to the seaboard next year by way of Port Colborne and the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. That will not be half or perhaps one-quarter of what will eventually go through our Canadian transportation routes. Large quantities will go from Depot Harbour and Midland, and I submit that if we expend $1,500,000 or even $2,000,000 at Port Colborne it will be an expenditure for the general good of Canada.
The subject is interesting and perli'aps the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) could tell us the length and width of those piers, and to what extent the work has progressed.

The piers are each GOO feet long by 200 feet wide. They were constructed by laying concrete walls on each side and the intention was to fill in the vacancy with loose stone that was dredged from the bottom of the harbour; the harbour being deepened from 14 or 18 feet to 21 feet. It has been stated by experts in elevator building that this loose stone would not make a satisfactory foundation for an elevator, and I am told by the Minister of Railways and Canals tlfat he has instructed the contractors to not put any more loose stone in there, and it will be decided very shortly what kind of foundation will be laid in order to allow of the erection of elevators on the piers.
What is the depth of water at these piers ?
Wlien tlie work is finished the depth will be 21 feet.
You have not 21 feet there now ?

The piers are built on the solid rock. The rock alongside of the piers is blasted bind taken out by the dredge. It would be useless to build concrete where the rock is, because the rock is as good a foundation as the concrete. They are building the piers on the rock foundation and all around the piers is deepened to 21 feet or 22 feet.
What would be the widtli of the basin formed between these piers and the opposite breakw'ater ?
Between the. outer end of the piers and the breakwater is 2,500 feet or 3,000 feet which leaves ample room for the largest boats tp turn in the basin provided the proper depth of water is afforded.
Is it the intention of the government to do any work this year at Grand Bend on the Lake Huron shore ?
That m'atter is under consideration. I can hardly tell the hon. gentleman what may be in the supplementary estimates, but it is under the consideration of the department.

Will the minister tell us why this item has been dropped from the estimates ? In 1900, at the time of the election, the government engineer went up there and made a survey and in the estimates for 1901, there was fan item of $5,700 inserted for this work. Since that, this item has been dropped out of the estimates altogether, and perhaps the minister can tell us why it has been dropped. I might state that this work would be very useful indeed. The fishermen for ten miles around come and fish at that point as it seems to be the best place for fishing in the district, 'and the completion of this work would be a great advantage to the fishing community.

The only reason the item was dropped was, that in preparing the main estimates for 1903-4, only estimates were included for works under way. I think you will find that there are no new works provided for in these estimates at 'all, and as this work was not under contract it was left over for consideration the same as all other items of a similar nature.
Has it been considered?
Yes, it is under consideration now.
In view of what the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has s'aid. might I ask what is the intention of the government with regard to constructing another breakwater at Port Colborne ?
It is quite impossible for me to make any promise as to what may be done until council decides what shall be put in the estimates.
Is it under the consideration of the department.

Certainly.
Sorel deep water wharf, $47,000.
Is this wharf built for the Richelieu and Onl'ario Navigation Company, or is it built for the public generally ?
My information is that it was built for the general public.

The object of this vote, as explained on a previous occasion, seems to have been to create an ocean port at Sorel for the purpose of doing a large export business. I understood, from the remarks of the Prime Minister on this subject last year, that the expenditure was very largely based on the fact that a considerable railway system had been developed in the vicinity of Sorel. Would the lion. Minister of Public Works tell us what the railway situation there is at the present time and to what extent it warrants a very large expenditure at this particular point for the purpose indicated.

There is no doubt that the building of this wharf was to provide deep water accommodation at that port. I believe the depth of water at this point is now thirty feet. I understand that the railway system on which Sorel depended so much has been somewhat unfortunate; but I am informed that it is under operation again. As to what the volume of trade will be, I am quite unable to say. I suppose there could not have been any tonnage there previous to. this accommodation being furnished. "Whether it will meet the expectation of those who advocate it, I am unable to say.

It looks as though from a vei-y small beginning, we were in for a pretty large expenditure on this matter. Last year, in answer to some inquiries which I made in regard to it, the Prime Minister stated that $25,000 was first voted for this work. The papers which have been brought down and laid on the Table of the House, show that the engineer of the department estimated that it would take $935,000 to carry out the various works for which petitions had been handed to the government. The Prime Minister. stated that the appropriation had been decided upon when the Minister of Public Works was absent from the city. As the amount voted was not sufficient, $100,000 was asked for and voted, and the Prime Minister stated that it would doubtless cost" $150,000 or $175,000 to complete this work. He said :

But railways are taking the place of waterways, and two railways are now converging at Sorel, the South Shore which has been constructed from Montreal to Sorel and beyond Sorel to Nicolet, and will be completed this year probably to LotbiniSre. There is the United Counties Railway also, which became the Rutland Railway, and which I believe now belongs to the New York Central, and it comes from the New York Central Railway system at Lake Champlain to the town of Sorel.
The papers which have been brought down show that the petitioners who were influential in getting the government to start this work were the United Counties Railway and the bank of St. Hyaeinthe. The petition of the United Counties Railway in one place says :
Your government will readily understand that, in order to induce steamers to dock at Sorel, large inducements will have to be given to them by the line of railway carrying the freight to that point, which will be a heavy charge upon this railway, and for this reason, among others, your petitioners confidently appeal to your government for support in their undertaking.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me the date of that petition ?

The letter transmitting it is dated Montreal, December 22, 1899, and is signed by Mr. J. N. Greenshields. The petition further says :
This road's plans are entirely contingent upon the completion of the dock, elevator and opening of the channel, and the building of several miles of railway leading to the docks, on or before the month of June of next year, and this company is prepared to complete such work as it may be properly expected to assume on or before that date, and confidently expects that your government, in the general interests of the country, and the development of its carrying trade, will accede to the requests of the present memorial.
The acting chief engineer of the department, Mr. Eugene D. Lafleur, made a report on the subject, which I will read in order that we may have an intelligent idea of what is before us :
Department of Public Works of Canada, Chief Engineer's Office,
Ottawa, January 10, 1900.
Sir,-With reference to file No. 208,734, being an application from Mr. J. N. Greenshields, on behalf of the United Counties Railway, for the construction of deep water terminal facilities at Sorel, I have the honour to state that a certain portion of the ground to be occupied by the improvements in question has already been surveyed by Mr. Assistant Engineer F. W. Cowie, and that judging from the estimate of the cost of the works then proposed, which only consisted of 1,000 feet of wharfing instead of the 2,000 feet applied for, the estimated cost of the works now required cannot be placed at a less figure than $935,000, as follows Dredging an area 800 feet wide by 25,000
feet in length, an average depth of 18
feet to 27| feet at extreme low water.. $255,000
-Cribwork and sheds	 430,000
Elevator of 1,000,000 bushels capacity.. 250'000 Mr. KEMP.
If the department decides to undertake this work it will of course be necessary to have a complete survey made, in order that the above estimate may be revised, especially as far as the dredging is concerned.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) EUGENE D. LAFLEUR,
Acting Chief Engineer.
The Secretary,
Department of Public Works.
Then, there is a petition from the city council of St. Hyaeinthe and a petition from the Bank of St. Hyaeinthe. There is si further report from the acting engineer, dated Ottawa, April 23, 1900, going into the matter more minutely. For, the dock at Sorel, which cost within about $5,000 of the estimate made by Mr. Lafleur, it suggests three sites. The site whicli he recommends would cost $200,330. There is nothing in these reports with reference to elevator facilities or dfedging a channel to the dock; but it must be assumed that if the government built the dock, they would have to provide a channel which would enable deep water steamers to reach the dock. So that what I said at the outset is apparently, that we are in for a tremendous expenditure for this work; and for my part, I do not see what benefit it will be to the country. When this matter was up before, it was said that these three railways converged at Sorel. But one of them only runs occasionally and sometimes does not run at all, and the statement of the Prime Minister about one of them becoming a part of the New York Central Railway was rather mythical and visionary; nothing has come of it. We have spent a good deal of money there, but I do not see what is the use of going on with the work. Sorel will never be able to compete as an ocean port with Quebec or Montreal. It is a river port and should have been left as such, and for my part I do not see why it should be necessary to throw away the resources of the country in an attempt to make it an ocean port.

My hon. friend will see that the total cost is $273,500, and the work is almost complete. What I am asking now is for $40,000 to pay the balance of the contract in full, so that whatever difference of opinion there may be as to the value of the work, it is now nearly completed and we have to pay for it.
Is this for a wharf ?

Yes.
Mr, GALLERY. Will the hon. minister tell us whether, after all the money we have spent to improve the St. Lawrence route, the insurance rates have been reduced ?
I cannot say whether any reduction has been made.

The rates have been very much decreased this year. The Canadian Pacific Railway fleet have obtained rates just as good as those in any other American port.
Ml'. GALLERY. And how is it that the Grand Trunk Railway can ship grain from Portland, 300 miles further than from Montreal, and cheaper than they can send it down the St. Lawrence ?

One reason is that we have no proper equipment in Montreal. The Grand Trunk Railway Company has an old elevator there and the Canadian Pacific Railway has two, but they are not modern elevators. The harbour commissioners are now building an elevator. Not only had we no modern elevators, but we had not handling facilities, and in fact we were not in it at all. I think that the rates this year will be as favourable as those at American ports. My hon. friend must not forget that perhaps competition was not as keen ns it might have been between the different companies, but now that the Canadian Pacific Railway can make cheap rates from west to east, other companies will follow suit. We must not forget also that grain is only a small portion of a steamer's cargo. A steamer takes as a rule about 50,000 bushels, so that if there are other competing trades as well, navigation companies will be in a condition to give better rates.
When we have thirty feet in the channel from Montreal to Quebec, how is it that there are so many accidents V Is the pilotage system bad or what is wrong ?

The hon. gentleman will find that last season there were very few accidents between Quebec and Montreal. The most of them were below Quebec. An accident happened to a man-of-war, but that ship grounded at a spot where the channel was 1,500 feet wide with fifty feet depth of water through a mistake of the pilot. Accidents of that kind will occur, but you cannot charge them against the St. Lawrence route. A week or two ago there was an accident because the buoys were either misplaced or displaced, and the pilot going between two buoys thought he was perfectly safe. Accidents like that cannot be explained, but there were no accidents last year between Quebec and Montreal worth mentioning. The channel is in good shape now. We have thirty feet of water all along the route at thisi period of the year, but after the 15th of September, when the water is low, there. will not be that depth. In a year or two, however,>
we will have that depth all through the season, and the ship channel is in better shape than it ever was-better buoys and better lighted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are wandering away from the item
which is for the construction of a wharf at Sorel.
This item speaks of a wharf, but I understood the hon. minister to say that it includes the dredging of the channel Is it for both ?
The contract is for the erection of a wharf but it includes dredging of the approach to the wharf.
The report of the engineer of the department contemplates an expenditure of $935,000.
That is all wrong. The total cost is $273,000, and this is to pay $47,000 which is the balance due to contractors.
What is this for ?
This is to build a wharf 700 feet long, forty-six feet high, and forty feet wide at the, base, and with thirty feet of water at low tide, together with 000 feet of trestle work.

This report contemplates an expenditure of $935,000, and the intention was to make Sorel an ocean port. Will this expenditure, which the hon. minister has mentioned, make Sorel a port for ocean vessels of the capacity of those which go to Montreal ? If that be the case, how can the minister account for this estimate of $935,000 ?
I never heard before of that estimate. We have to deal with the plan adopted and not with estimates which often vary.
According to this report, the work should cost $900,000.
That is an old report and was never acted upon.
The hon. gentleman will not say that when the money is expended and the contract completed, we shall have an ocean port for large vessels.

I do not see that there is any doubt about it. There will be thirty feet of water and probably the largest vessels can stop there.
I am told that when this is finished, there will be 1,300 feet of wharfage, which will give facilities for two of the largest boats.
Who will build the elevator referred to in the report ?
That is another question.
Are there any prospects of using the port for ocean vessels and utilizing the railways that were referred to ?
The local people seem to think that trade will come there.
What does the hon. minister think ?

The minister may be like my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) perhaps, not a very good authority, but optimistic, with great confidence in Canada and with great hope that all these ports will be successful in the near future.

No doubt, when this matter was put before the House by the Prime Minister last session it was represented to be in somewhat different shape from that in which the Minister of Public Works finds it to-night. The Prime Minister said :
Now, the intention is to make Sorel an ocean port.
And, at the conclusion of his remarks he
says :
This

That is, this expenditure

-is not only for Sorel but it is part of the system to equip the harbours of Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec. I am sure that my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Kemp) has no doubt whatever that before many years there will be enough trade coming from Ontario and the west to supply all those harbours, of which Sorel is one.	.
Does the hon. Minister of Public Works desire to commit us to a scheme of that kind to-night ? Is it not plain that Montreal and Quebec are not getting one-tenth of the trade they ought to have; and, while that state of affairs exists, are we to equip this third ocean port on the St. Lawrence without the slightest probability so far as any one can see of its being of any use for the purpose within the lifetime of any of us ? This rote may be to pay the contractors, but what is the intention of the government with regard to the project itself? My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Kemp) reasonably asks : Who is going to build the elevator, which must be built if Sorel is to do the trade of the west along with or instead of Montreal or Quebec ? Does the government commit itself to the project of establishing Sorel as a port to do the grain business of the west ? One would suppose that that was so absolutely visionary that the hon. minister would not commit himself to it. Or, perhaps, he will do so. This extensive work that is being done seems altogether too large for local traffic, but entirely inadequate, without additional enormous expenditure in the future, for doing any of this proposed grain business from the west. This whole expenditure of a quarter of a million of dollars seems based upon the theory that these railways are to be part of a very important system, but that portion of the scheme seems to have absolutely broken down. In any case, the railway system with which it is proposed to connect Sorel, from what I can gather from the debate of last Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
year, would direct the grain trade toward New York instead of Sorel. Of course, I do not speak by the book with regard to that. I think that before we pass this item the Minister of Public Works ought to be frank with the House and tell us whether he thinks it is a justifiable expenditure for the purposes of local traffic; or, if there is something more than that, and, if as the Prime Minister stated last year, this is to be an ocean port to take the grain trade of the west, where is our expenditure to stop, and what reasonable prospect is there in the mind of any of us that Sorel can ever compete with Montreal or Quebec, and what reason is there it should be required to do so ?

This is a considerable expenditure for a wharf for local trade. But, of course, it has created an ocean port, if that is the term to apply to a port where you have a depth of thirty feet of water. As to the expectations formed, as my hon. friend has pointed out, that a great railway system, as was represented by the government, would do so much, it seems to have met with some mishap and the prospect is not so bright for the grain trade as it appeared at that time. The contract was entered into on June 25, 1901, and the work has been almost completed. No matter what my views may be as to the future prospects of Sorel, I think that there can be no doubt that we are called upon to pay the contractors the amount due. I am not in position to say what the future of this railway system, concerning which such representations were made to the government, may be. But, of course, we hope for the best.

It seems to amount to this-that the hon. minister thinks there is not very much in this, but we are committed to it to the extent of $240,000. and we must pay a debt which the government contracted without very much justification. I am very sorry indeed that the right hon. the Prime Minister is not able to be here to-night. I am not complaining of that, because I know we cannot expect him to be here always. But I do think the hon. Minister of Public Works had better let the item stand until the Prime Minister is here, and we can then have some explanation from him, for, no doubt, he is more familiar with the matter than the Minister of Public Works is. I think it must be pretty apparent that the position the right hon. Prime Minister took last year is not a very strong one, to say the least. But he may be able to give us some explanation which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works does seem to be able to give. But I think it is not unreasonable to ask that the item be allowed to stand in the meantime. Of course, if we are to say that every place on the St. Lawrence where you get thirty feet of water is to be equipped as an ocean port, and a quarter

of a million, or a million or two million dollars must be spent there, we will all agree that that is a pretty plain proposition, but I do not know how far the Minister of Public Works would commend it as a sensible or a reasonable proposition. And there does not seem to be much in the proposition with regard to Sorel, that goes beyond that. I am willing to expend public money on Sorel, or anywhere else, if it is in the interest of the country to do so. But to expend a quarter of a million dollars there under present circumstances is really too absurd for us to discuss. We kaye got to decide what are to be the great ocean ports for our grain trade from the west, and it is our duty to equip them in order to keep that trade of our own country for the ports of our own country. But it seems to me that we are only handicapping our interests if, while leaving Montreal and Quebec and other ports which have a prospect of getting this trade, comparatively unequipped, we are to spend money in projects of this kind which have not any reasonable foundation, and which depend for any possibility of success upon schemes with regard to railways which have not had any success at all, and which have no probability or possibility of success except in the minds of certain railway promoters. I do not want to put this matter too strongly ; but I have not heard anything from my hon. friend which convinces me that my view is a wrong one. It seems to me this sum is altogether too large to be expended at this place, unless "you propose to equip it as an ocean port; and how can you justify the project of equipping it as an ocean port for the grain trade of the west, in view of the situation as it has developed there ? Under these circumstances does the Minister of Public Works not think that some better explanation is due to the House before we should be called upon to vote this item.

Perhaps the proposition of the leader of the opposition is a reasonable one. I have only to say that we have spent a great deal of the time of the session discussing this question on various occasions. Perhaps the Prime Minister will make a statement and answer any question in regard to it.

We know that the hon. gentleman has had a good deal of discussion over his estimates, but I want to remind him that to-night we have been voting money at the rate of $5,000 a minute, according to a calculation I made a short time ago. So. for once in his life, he ought to be satisfied with the progress which has been made. Perhaps the views which I have presented to him may strike him as reasonable.
Before we leave that item, I would like to ask the minister if he would state the amounts that have been paid to these contractors since they signed that contract.

The amounts paid up to the 30th of September, were $178,788.81. The total amount that will be paid up to the 30th of June will be $226,500. There remains a balance of $47,000. Does the leader of the opposition want this item to stand ?

I do not want to interfere with any discussion that might affect the disposal of the item. If any hon. gentleman has anything to say about the item he might go on and say it. But I would like it to stand eventually in order that we may get some explanation from the Prime Minister of the situation from his standpoint.

Let it stand.
Item allowed to stand.
St. Joseph, Lake Huron-wharf, $5,000.
Is it the intention of the minister to spend that money on this wharf this year ?

If the item is voted and we undertake to complete the work, it will probably be expended this year. The question to be decided is whether the work should be abandoned or whether the $5,000 now asked for should be voted and spent. The ex-Minister of Public Works mentioned the other night, when some objection was taken to the item, that he would look into the matter and that he had recommended the work to be gone on with. But now some exception is taken as to the value of the work.

When the item came before the House last year I pledged myself not to go on with the work without being there. In my absence, during the Paris exposition, some gentlemen from Montreal and St. Joseph came to Ottawa on a deputation to the Prime Minister, who promised them to look carefully into this question. He ordered a survey, as he was replacing me to a large extent in the department, so far as the province of Quebec was concerned. A survey had been made when I came back. I also pledged myself to look into the question and I did so. After the session was over last year I went to St. Joseph and found out what perhaps I might have found by looking at the map, that between Goderich and Sarnia there are thirty miles of coast without any wharf, except at Bayfield, around which there is scarcely any water. This is a wharf that has not been used very much in the past because there has been no available depth of water. But, Waving ascertained these facts I made up my mind that the work would be a most useful one, not to St. Joseph alone, but to the surrounding population that would lie put in a position to trade with that point. There are different interests, I know, which are opposed to the building of this work. Those who have interests in the villages

behind are naturally opposed to the building of a wharf there. Hum'an nature is the same everywhere in the world. I know some of our friends have stores and interests at the station and they are opposed to the building of a wharf. A Minister of the Crown has not to look at these small interests. He has to look at the general interests. I made up iny mind tb'at it would be a good thing to have a wharf between Sarnia and Goderich. I ordered a survey. Mr. Corriveau, a well known and energetic engineer, made the survey. His report is in the department and it has been confirmed by Mr. Roy, who was then inspector general of public works. The work was to cost a little over $5,000. Under these conditions I ordered the work to be proceeded with. I am very much surprised to hear that it will cost $15,000. I understand there have been accidents. I entrusted the work to Mr. Sing, one of the most experienced engineers in the service of the department. I do not exactly remember the name of the foreman, but Mr. Sing was in charge. X understand that the work, not being completed, was partly carried away by the waves. That, of course has contributed to the increased cost of the work. St. Joseph is a little French village. It is a little French spot. There have always been little French spots over this Canadian laud of ours. There are some industries already there. It is not a large village, but it is a very nice place, very picturesque and very nicely located indeed. I think that the building of a wharf would be a source of development and progress. It will serve not only the village of St. Joseph, but the population around. I would be sorry to see the work abandoned. It has cost a great deal more than I expected it would cost, because the estimate which was in my hands when the work was started was that the cost would-be a little over $5,000. Part of the money is spent and it seems to me tli'at the work should he carried out. Of course my hon. friend has now charge of the Department of Public Works, and if he believes the work should be abandoned it is his right to abandon it.
Mr. MeEWEN. Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the government to allow this matter to stand over for another year. You have heard what the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has said about this village. These men who have this village in charge talk very large ; in fact, very much larger than they will ever do. I do not wish to say anything against them but I would like this item to be left over for another year to see if they will carry out their undertakings. They have not yet established a manufactory of any kind or any other thing that would require 'a wharf. I would be the first one to assist them in getting it if there was any necessity for it, but there is not a single commodity of product there to be brought in or sent out.

There is not a manufactory of any kind that is running. They have a sawmill and a number of other buildings. It is true that they have a hotel building 150 feet by 150 feet, but it is there high and dry and there is nothing for it to do. As to the wharf there has been $10,000 spent and I am very sorry to say that the money has been unwisely spent. There are seven or eight cribs on the shore and one crib in two or three feet of water and that is the whole result of the expenditure of $10,000.
I know whereof I speak, as I have been there and have seen it. When I was there Mr. Cantin, the promoter of the village, told me that there had been 200 or 300 cords of stone gathered up along the shore but when I looked along the shore I could see no stone gathered up. There is a quantity of timber which has not been fixed up. In the meantime I think the government should allow the matter to remain in abeyance for another year so as to see if the promoters of this village will go on with their undertakings. If they do so, and if they show that they mean business I will be the first one to help them. But, under the present circumstances, I could not approve of this expenditure because nine out of ten of my constituents believe that the money has been unwisely expended.

Perli'aps the lion. Minister of Public Works will allow me to say that there has been a strong company formed to purchase the different properties and works that were initiated a couple of years ago by Mr. Cantin. I know the men in Montreal who are in this company and they 'are very substantial men. One of them is at the head of the very well known firm of Damontagne & Company, one of the very . largest firms in Montreal. The company that has been formed to develop the little village that was started two or three years, is a substantial company.
Is it not an American company ?	*
No, it is a Canadian company, mostly composed of French Canadians.
That is a work of encoui'age-meut ?

That is no reason why they should not be encouraged. They are good people when they are working for the development of the country, and it seems to me that the province of Ontario which has been losing population should not prevent French Canadians from settling there.
I think if I appeal on this ground to my hon. friends on both sides of the House my voice will be heard with a certain amount of sympathy. I would appeal to the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McEwen). These people will become his best electors. I would invite him to withdraw his objection to the work. He says that he will wait and

see what these people will do. The way to help them Is to give them a wharf. If you do not give them the means of communication they might not carry out as successfully as they expect the work they have undertaken. The work has been undertaken. An accident has happened. This is not the first wharf in a difficult place where an accident has happened. Other works have been carried away but have been built all the same. Under the circumstances, I think that my hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) would be wise in withdrawing his objection. Of course the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) is responsible for the administration of his department, but lam giving my advice to the best of my knowledge, and it seems to me that the House should feel kindly towards those who have invested their money there. A big hotel was built there at a cost of $250,000 I am told, but it was a failure. There are two or three small factories, but I grant they are not big.
What about the bricks they were to manufacture, and that they were to ship to Chicago.
They are manufacturing bricks there now.
Are they sending them to Chicago ?

They will when they have a wharf. There is no wharf between Sarnia and Goderich, a distance of thirty miles, except at Bayfield, where there is no water. It seems to me that the House should not hesitate to spend this small sum of money.

I would have raised my voice against this vote last year, only I never dreamt, and no one in that part of the country ever dreamt, that when the Hon. Mr. Tarte went up there and saw the place he would spend the money. The hon. gentleman promised to come my way and we would go out together and see it, but instead of that he went by way of Parkhill and he was there only two hours and we never saw a sight of him. The great majority of even the French people who are there never asked for this money. It is true that the people who put money into that scheme have lost their money and will never see a cent of it again. Mr. Cantin has a peculiar way with him and he seems to succeed in making people give their money to put into enterprises that could never produce a cent. What surprises me is that a man of his kind should be able to mislead this government into spending money where there is no need for it at the present time or for years to come, any more than there is any need of building a wharf on the top of a mountain. If this wharf is built it will be built at the foot of a hill where there is no way to get at it unless you buy land
from some one, unless there will be a road built through a gulch that is a very hard place to get at. In the meantime they make the road through somebody's land, and they get around to it in that way, but where this dock is being built there is a hill about fifty feet high. It is not quite straight up, but nearly so, and it will be very hard to get at it suppose the dock is built. With all due regard to the engineers, $5,000 is not worth anything to build a wharf there.

So far as the hill is concerned my hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) knows that'it is an easy thing to have a slanting road there. I went down the hill myself and there is already a road there. My hon. friend has reproached me for not having called on him when I went there.
You promised to.
I will tell my reason frankly to tile House.
I want to hear it.
My hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) showed himself very favourable to the work when he was talking to these men.
To what men.
Well, to Mr. Cantin and others and my hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) had written to me that he was not favourable to it. I always deal straight with men.
Did you deal straight with me when you did not come to see me as yon promised ?

My hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) had written to me that he did not like the work while he had said to other people that he was favourable to the work, and under those circumstances I made up my mind to judge for myself, what any other minister would have done. Bet us deal frankly and fairly between man and man. I fully made up my mind to judge for myself. My hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) moreover, had been elected as an independent member of the House against Mr. MacMillan, an old Liberal that we all respected here. My hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) was not looked upon as a straight supporter of the government. He was an independent member of parliament, having been elected against a strong Liberal, who sat for years in this House. Under the circumstances I thought that without meaning offence to the hon. gentleman, I was justified in going there as I had pledged myself to the House I would, and see for myself. The site of the wharf has been chosen with the greatest care, and it is easy indeed to get access to it. A big storm has carried away part of the work and it has increased the cost. I repeat that a strong company has been formed ; the little village has been divided into lots; there are two or three small

factories; there is a brick factory; there is a pipe organ factory; I grant it is not a large place, but we have built wharfs in other parts of the country in places that were not very large.

This man is no doubt a good deal of the character the hon. gentleman (Mr. McEwen) spoke of. He seems to be able to live by his wits and to induce people to put money in schemes that have little foundation. I do not know him myself or anything about him except what I have heard in~comiection with tliis matter. He deceived a great many people into putting money into this scheme. It is stated now that a good many substantial people have taken hold of the work, and I think we might probably take the vote and spend it on the conditions as to whether they are going on to develop this place and the work will help to do so. Now that we have spent so much money we might go on.

And aid him to deceive others.
Mr. MeEWEN. The ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says that I was elected as an independent. I wish to deny that statement in toto. I wish to say that the speech which I made at Seaforth tlie day of the nomination did not say anything to the effect that I was an independent. I have a copy of my speeches at home and I can produce them at any time, and they will show that the Hon. Mr. Tarte is not well informed about that. So far as the spending of the money is concerned, you can go on and spend the money if you like, but you will not do it with my consent. I voice the opinion of nine out of ten people, not only in my riding, but in the whole county, and I think my representations should have some attention paid to them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You seem to be an independent.

This is an extraordinary state of affairs when we find the government going into the riding of a member who supports them and spending money there contrary to his wishes. It does seem to me that there is not a precedent for this to be found in the Dominion of Canada. I have listened with considerable interest to what was said by the hon. member (Mr. McEwen) and also what was said by the ex-minister who has referred to there being a French settlement at that place. I am very glad to be able to say that there is a small French settlement there, and I wish there were more of the same kind of people. They are an intelligent and industrious people, and I can assure the hon. minister that they are no more in favour of throwing away money in this way than the rest of us. It is news to me, as the hon. ex-minister told us to-night, that there was $10,000 spent last year at that point, because, if I remember rightly, $5,000 was the amount placed Hon. Mr. TARTE.
in the estimates last year, and from what I have heard of the amount of work, done there, and the way it was done, I think the people of that part of the country considered that $5,000, or even a much less sum, spent on that work, was very improperly spent. I have not visited the place; but when listening to the discussion to-night, it occurred to me that asi there is a hill there, it is a pity the wharf was not built on the top of the hill; for it would have served as useful a purpose as it does now, and the government would have been in a much better position to move it away and utilize it in some other part of the country. The exMinister of Public Works said there were men of capital behind this scheme. I can tell him that there were, and they have not now as much capital as they had before. I do not wish to make this statement to hurt the feelings of the man who was the chief mover in this work; but one of our wealthiest men lost his money in that enterprise, and died, I will not say a pauper, but very much poorer than he would have been if he had not met the gentleman who was pushing that scheme. I am stating not merely my own opinion, but the opinion of every intelligent man, whether Liberal or Conservative, who knows what the St. Joseph wharf is, when I say that when this expenditure is mentioned, it is looked upon as a ridiculous expenditure. I do not wish to say this in the way of criticising the government, because if that wharf were going to be of any benefit to that part of the country, I am sure that my hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McEwen) and myself would be the last men to stand up in this House and ask that the item be dropped, because it is in a part of the country in which we are both much interested. As for any enterprise going forward at that point, there has not been any and there will not be any. I do not think the hon. exMinister of Public Works will stand up here and say that an expenditure of $15,000 or $20,000 will build a wharf at that place. Bayfield is a natural harbour, where work could be carried on, but St. Joseph is on an open beach, at about as exposed a place on the Lake Huron shore as it would be possible to find. I think all hon. members will agree with me that $15,000 or $20,000 is of no use to build a harbour there; and even if a harbour were built, I can assure you that it would serve no purpose. I am sorry the item was ever placed in the estimates. The money already spent there has been thrown away, and if the government spend any more there, it will be thrown away also. I can do nothing less than to move that the Item be struck out.

Perhaps the hon. Minister of Public Works will tell the House how much money has been spent at Bayfield. My hon. friend (Mr. Sherritt) should not forget that there is no harbour there. He knows that between Sarnia and Goderich

for a distance of thirty miles, there is no harbour. I know he has been voting side by side with my hon. friend from South Huron (McEwen) against that wharf; I knew they were a unit against it. There are not many parts of the country in such an important portion of Canada as that district is where there is a coast of thirty miles without a wharf. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do; but still, because the place-, is called St. Joseph, my hon. friends are dead against it.
No, no.

Well, I express my views as I believe them to be. I really believe it, because I call the attention of the House and the country to this fact, that in a distance of thirty miles there is not a wharf available, and there is a large population of about 30,000 people in that distinct who will use that wharf later on. There is a large trade there. But there are two reasons why the wharf is opposed : First, because the little place is called St. Joseph; and, second, because there are interests at the station and at Hensall and Zurich which are opposed to that wharf, because they think it will drive business from them. These are the interests that have raised opposition to this little work, about which I think there should not be so much fuss.

I am sorry that our hon. friend the late Minister of Tublic Works seems to think that we are opposed to this work because the people there are French. I! wish to inform him and the House that there is nothing in that, and I am sorry that my hon. friend, I was going to say, was foolish enough to say so. The people who were imported there by Mr. Cantin are waiting to get their money back from him. Whether in municipal elections or in other elections these people have been my very best friends. With regard to the position of Hensall and Zurich, I cannot speak for Zurich, but I am sure that the people of Hensall never thought of opposing this wharf because it would take business from them. That idea never entered into the question at all. There might be some opposition to a railroad on that account ; but so far as the lake is concerned, $15,000 or $20,000 will build no wharf at that point that will be worth ten cents to any vessel that may come there. It is on the open lake, where there is a sweep of about 200 miles from the Northwest and about sixty miles from the west, and a single pier running out 200 or 300 feet in shallow water is not worth ten cents for any boat to come to. No sailing vessel will come there except at the very finest time of the year, and no steam barge will come there, because it is so close to the shore. As regards opposition to these French people, there is nothing in it and that charge is an absurd falsehood. These people are our best friends and there are none we would sooner help, but in that regard there
is nothing to be done at present. In fact there is nothing doing there. I am aware that there is one man who makes pipe organs for the churches, and be is a very decent fellow who works all the time and apart from that industry, there is a small brick and tile works.
I know7 that there is a great deal of difference of opinion with regard to this.
Not in Huron.

There has been over $10,000 expended on the work, but I am perfectly willing, if the item passes, to have an inquiry into all the circumstances, and if this work is not in the public interest, I will not finish it. The chief engineer of the department says that there are ten or eleven feet of water there, and I cannot understand how he could have made such a report if there is none.
As far as I am personally concerned, if the hon. minister will go up there and see for himself, I am willing to let the item drop.
If the hon. gentleman thinks that I should go instead of the chief engineer, I am quite willing to do so.

Before the item passes, I want to put myself right. The ex-Minister of Public Works has said that I am opposed to this expenditure because the place is called St. Joseph. That sort of thing may make an impression in this House, but he would have considerable difficulty in getting the people of that locality to take any stock in it. The hon. gentleman is a little short of the distance because it is longer than he makes it out, between Goderich and Sarnia, but there is a place, some six or seven miles below that, for which an appropriation was made in 1891, and which is an old place of considerable Importance, wrhere there are mills and considerable business done, and where besides the municipality have spent $20,000 in straightening the river. I refer to Grand Bend. There was an item of $5,700 put iuto the estimates of 1901 for the purpose of dredging the river there, but that item lias been dropped. I can assure the hqn. minister that that is a work the people consider necessary, as the place is a fishing point which would be very valuable if proper accommodation were furnished. Besides, there is a good sawmill running there and considerable timber, and it is a very extensive summer resort. That is a place where work should be done, and I am glad that the hon. minister has promised to consider the advisability of putting in an item in the supplementaries for that purpose. We are further from market there than at St. Joseph, and it is a much easier place to build a breakwater and a harbour. I am satisfied that if the hon. minister will go

there and will look into the matter carefully, he will see that it is a place where an expenditure would be a good investment.

I am perfectly willing to go up there and consult the hon. members of the riding before anything further is done.
Item voted.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Postmaster General, House adjourned at 12.10 a.m. Wednesday.

Wednesday, May 20, 1903.
